name: GHC Haskell lightweight threads (skynet 1M-spawn benchmark vs pthread/std::thread)
baseline: pthread_create and std::thread (C/C++ OS threads, 8 kB pthread stacks) running the skynet recursive spawn-and-sum benchmark
workload: skynet microbenchmark: a root unit spawns 10 children, each spawns 10 more, down to 1,000,000 leaves that return their ordinal; sums flow back up; time per spawned unit (GHC thread versus OS thread).
claimed_speedup: Haskell (stack-1.4.0/ghc-8.0.1): 0.05-0.06 us per unit (average over 1,000,000) versus pthread 54-73 us, std::thread 52-73 us and std::async 106-122 us per thread (average over 10,000, because 1,000,000 OS threads exhausted resources): about 870x-1,460x lower per-unit cost (derived from page data; sizes differ). The same page shows Boost.Fiber (C++, 16C/32T, work stealing, tcmalloc) at 0.05-0.09 us per fiber, so C++ user-space fibers match the Haskell row.
compiler_and_flags: C++ side (page): gcc-6.3.1, Boost.Build variant=release optimization=speed (-O3), pthreads created with 8 kB stacks, std::thread with the system default 1-2 MB stacks, glibc malloc or tcmalloc (-ltcmalloc). Haskell side (page): stack-1.4.0 / ghc-8.0.1 only. The skynet repo's haskell/skynet.cabal sets ghc-options -O2 -threaded -rtsopts and its README runs 'stack exec skynet +RTS -N', but the Boost page does not say which Haskell variant or RTS options it used.
hardware: dual Intel Xeon E5-2620 v4 2.2 GHz, 16C/32T, 64 GB RAM, Linux x86_64
stars_or_usage: 3.3k stars (github.com/ghc/ghc is a read-only mirror of gitlab.haskell.org/ghc/ghc, which was not opened)
tradeoffs: GHC threads are heap-allocated stack chunks scheduled by the GHC runtime (garbage-collected, optional -threaded and -N). Foreign calls and unsafe FFI interact with the scheduler differently from C.
caveats: Variant mismatch (main finding): atemerev/skynet haskell/src/Main.hs runs five implementations under criterion (Parallel, MVar, Chan, TBQueue, Unagi); its own comments give, on an i7-4930K with +RTS -N6, Parallel 0.017 s and MVar 1.7 s per 1,000,000-leaf run. The Boost row (0.05-0.06 us x 1,000,000 = 50-60 ms) matches the Parallel variant's order of magnitude, not the forkIO+MVar one (inference; the page does not name the variant). Parallel.hs computes a pure tree sum with parMap rpar: it creates sparks (work-stealing pool entries the parent may evaluate itself), no forkIO threads and no channel messages, whereas the C++ port (boostorg/fiber performance/thread/skynet_pthread.cpp) creates about 11,110 detached pthreads for its 10,000 leaves and passes every value through a mutex/condition-variable buffered_channel. So the comparison is sparks (or green threads) against kernel threads, not the same work, and the win is the runtime's, not Haskell codegen's. Scale differs (1,000,000 units for Haskell, 10,000 for pthread/std::thread). The skynet README's own Haskell (GHC 7.10.3) results range from 41-44 ms (i7-4771, Ubuntu) to 2820-6181 ms (Windows, OS X), consistent with different variants being run. Toolchains date from 2017 (go1.8.1, ghc-8.0.1, erts-8.3, gcc-6.3.1). The baseline is OS threads, not the idiomatic C++ answer for massive concurrency; Boost.Fiber on the same page reaches 0.05-0.09 us. No Haskell benchmark code lives in boostorg/fiber (performance/ holds only fiber/ and thread/). The repo_url is the GHC mirror (gitlab.haskell.org/ghc/ghc is upstream); the skynet sources are MIT, last commit 2023-11-10. GHC's licence file is the Glasgow Haskell Compiler License (BSD-3-Clause text).
found_via: WebSearch: 'lightweight threads comparison goroutines vs pthreads creation time Go faster than C pthreads paper evaluation' surfaced the Boost.Fiber performance page; the Haskell row is on the same page.
why_faster: Implied by the page rather than argued: GHC threads are runtime-scheduled green threads, pthreads are OS threads. No explicit mechanism is given.

verification.tier_reason: boostorg/fiber doc/performance.qbk (Boost.Fiber author, independent of GHC) shows Haskell 0.05-0.06 us per unit at 1,000,000 units against pthread 54-73 us and std::thread 52-73 us at 10,000 threads on a stated Xeon E5-2620 v4 with gcc-6.3.1 release/speed, but the Haskell build flags, RTS options and which of the five skynet Haskell variants ran are unstated, the gain is ~870-1,460x (cap at C for >50x with unstated flags), and the two sides run at different sizes and very likely different algorithms. Not A (no Haskell flags), not B (unequal workloads, unknown variant).
verification.notes: Downgrade B to C: numbers are on the Boost.Fiber page, but the Haskell row very likely measured the parMap/rpar spark variant (no threads, no channels) against one detached pthread per unit, at different sizes (1M vs 10k) and with Haskell flags unstated. Shortcomings to record: different algorithm (sparks vs kernel threads), unequal workload sizes, Haskell variant/flags/RTS options unstated, 2017 toolchains, C++ fibers on the same page match Haskell so no language-level win. baseline_stdlib set to libstdc++ (gcc-6.3.1 on Linux runs std::thread/std::async from libstdc++).

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: Haskell (stack-1.4.0/ghc-8.0.1): 0.05-0.06 us per thread (average over 1,000,000) versus pthread 54-73 us and std::thread 52-73 us per thread (average over 10,000): about 900x-1,460x lower cost per unit (derived from page data).
corrected_fields.compiler_and_flags: C++ side: gcc-6.3.1, Boost.Build variant=release optimization=speed (pthreads created with 8 kB stacks); Haskell side: stack-1.4.0 / ghc-8.0.1, flags not stated
corrected_fields.caveats: The baseline is OS threads (pthread_create, std::thread), not the idiomatic C++ answer for massive concurrency. The same page shows Boost.Fiber (C++ user-space fibers, work stealing, tcmalloc) at 0.05-0.09 us per fiber, which matches or beats Go and Erlang, so this is not a claim that the language beats well-tuned C++. Scale differs: the Go/Haskell/Erlang rows average over 1,000,000 spawned units while the pthread/std::thread rows average over only 10,000 threads because the 1,000,000-thread run exhausted resources (so the ratio compares per-unit cost at different sizes). The numbers come from the Boost.Fiber author's own documentation, ported skynet code for the C++ side (performance/thread/skynet_pthread.cpp: detached pthreads plus a mutex and condition-variable buffered channel) versus the upstream Go source's unbuffered channels; toolchains are from 2017 (go1.8.1, ghc-8.0.1, erts-8.3, gcc-6.3.1). Go/Haskell/Erlang compile flags and runtime options (for example GHC +RTS -N) are not stated on the page. The per-language skynet sources are in https://github.com/atemerev/skynet (MIT, last commit 2023-11-10). Tier B, not A, because the workload sizes differ and the non-C++ flags are unstated; rerunning at an equal unit count would settle it. The repo_url is the GHC compiler mirror because the claim is about the compiler/runtime; the skynet Haskell source is haskell/ in atemerev/skynet. The license file is the Glasgow Haskell Compiler License (BSD-3-Clause text).

name: NPB-Rust (NAS Parallel Benchmarks in Rust, sequential and Rayon)
baseline: NPB-CPP, the group's C++ port of NAS Parallel Benchmarks 3.4.1 (sequential NPB-SER, and OpenMP NPB-OMP for the parallel comparison), plus the original Fortran NPB
workload: NAS Parallel Benchmarks kernels EP, CG, MG, IS, FT and pseudo-applications BT, SP, LU in Rust (sequential NPB-RUST and Rayon-parallel NPB-RAYON), compared with the C++ and Fortran versions.
claimed_speedup: From the paper abstract as shown in a search snippet (snippet only): Rust sequential is 5.59% faster than C++ and 1.23% slower than Fortran; Rust with Rayon is slower than both the Fortran and the C++ OpenMP versions.
compiler_and_flags: Repo defaults (paper's actual compilers and flags not seen): Rust 1.85.0+, RUSTFLAGS='--cfg class="X"' cargo build --release with no [profile] section in NPB-RUST/Cargo.toml (opt-level 3, no LTO, no target-cpu); C++ NPB-CPP NPB-SER/config/make.def: g++ -std=c++14 with CFLAGS -O3 -mcmodel=medium; Fortran compiler and flags unknown.
tradeoffs: Rust port of NPB with a sequential variant (NPB-RUST) and a Rayon variant (NPB-RAYON); safety and ergonomics trade-offs are not discussed on the pages that were opened.
caveats: The arXiv page (2502.15536) is blocked in this environment and was not opened; the numbers come from WebSearch snippets of arxiv.org/html/2502.15536v1 (snippet only), so venue, peer-review status, hardware, compiler versions and per-kernel results are unconfirmed; a verifier with paper access should retier. The GitHub repo has no performance numbers. The only win over C++ is the sequential aggregate (5.59%, a small margin); Rayon is slower than C++ OpenMP and Fortran OpenMP, so the concurrency-runtimes category fits poorly (the win is sequential codegen, closer to numerics). The C++ baseline is the same group's NPB-CPP port (FGCS 2021, https://github.com/GMAP/NPB-CPP). Public build defaults are equivalent in optimisation level (-O3 against cargo --release opt-level 3, neither with -march=native), but the C++ default adds -mcmodel=medium; whether that or anything else explains the 5.59% is untested. The latest commit (2026-10-08, 3bb2455 'fix: adjusted tolrsd constants in LU') only assigns the 1.0e-08 tolrsd constants that were previously left at zero; with zero tolerances the early-exit residual check never fired, so the measured LU did the full iteration count and the fix does not inflate the published numbers. NPB-Rust has a --cfg safe="true" switch whose default (unset) reports UNSAFE=true; which mode the paper timed is not stated.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Rust Rayon vs C++ OpenMP TBB performance comparison paper NAS Parallel Benchmarks Rust faster' surfaced arXiv 2502.15536; opened the GMAP/NPB-Rust and GMAP/NPB-CPP repos.

verification.tier_reason: arXiv 2502.15536 is unreachable here (DNS/egress blocked); the 5.59%-faster-than-C++ sequential aggregate and the Rayon-slower-than-OpenMP result were seen only in a WebSearch snippet of arxiv.org/html/2502.15536v1 (snippet only). The paper is by the same group that wrote both NPB-Rust and the NPB-CPP baseline, peer review is unconfirmed (README cites arXiv only), and hardware and compiler versions were not seen, so first-party tier C stands.
verification.notes: Confirm at C: repo, MIT licence, 31 stars and 2026-10-08 last commit check out; paper numbers seen only in a search snippet (arXiv blocked), first-party, small 5.59% aggregate sequential margin, Rayon loses to OpenMP. Shortcomings to record: snippet-only evidence, same-group C++ baseline, unknown hardware/compiler versions, weak category fit (sequential win filed under concurrency-runtimes).

corrected_fields.compiler_and_flags: Rust: toolchain 1.85.0 or newer, cargo build --release (repo README); C++ and Fortran compilers and flags unknown
corrected_fields.caveats: The arXiv page (2502.15536) is blocked in this environment and was not opened; the numbers come from a WebSearch snippet of arxiv.org/html/2502.15536v1 (snippet only), so the venue, peer-review status, hardware and flags are unconfirmed and a verifier with paper access should retier. The GitHub repo page has no performance numbers. The only win over C++ is the sequential aggregate (5.59%, a small margin); the concurrency part (Rayon versus C++ OpenMP) is a loss, so the category fit is weak and the entry belongs more to numerics/safety if kept. name: Tokio (1M concurrent tasks, peak memory)
baseline: Asio C++20 coroutines (awaitable tasks) and concurrencpp
workload: Spawn N concurrent async tasks that wait on a timer and measure peak memory (port of the Rust '1 million concurrent tasks' memory benchmark to C++ coroutine libraries).
claimed_speedup: Peak memory at 1M tasks: tokio 214,136 KB, concurrencpp 605,972 KB, Asio 853,144 KB (about 2.8x and 4.0x less, derived from page data); at 100k tasks: 23,824 vs 61,460 vs 86,652 KB; at 10k: 6,908 vs 7,840 vs 10,244 KB. At 1 task tokio is the largest (3,092 KB vs Asio 1,668 KB). Libunifex hangs at 100k and 1M.
compiler_and_flags: C++20, CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Release set in CMakeLists.txt (-O3 -DNDEBUG with GCC or Clang), compiler not named; Asio and concurrencpp fetched by FetchContent with no GIT_TAG (default-branch HEAD at build time, June 2023), libunifex GIT_TAG main; tokio_bench built by 'cargo build --release' from CMakeLists.txt (opt-level 3), tokio 1.28.2 per Cargo.lock, #[tokio::main] multi-thread runtime.
hardware: Intel i7-8550U (8 threads, about 1.99 GHz), 8 GB RAM, WSL Ubuntu 20.04.6 on Windows 10
tradeoffs: Tokio tasks are stackless futures sized by the compiler, so memory is small per task but not free of heap allocation per spawn; the C++ libraries allocate a coroutine frame per task. The result is about memory only, not throughput or latency.
caveats: Independent hobby replication (4 stars, 6 commits all on 2023-06-24) of the pkolaczk 'How Much Memory Do You Need to Run 1 Million Concurrent Tasks?' benchmark, not the tokio authors' work; the README notes the original methodology was criticised. Memory only (peak RSS from /usr/bin/time), no timing; run count not stated; WSL Ubuntu 20.04 on a laptop i7-8550U with 8 GB. C++ compiler unnamed and Asio/concurrencpp versions unpinned. Workloads match logically (N tasks each awaiting a 10 s timer, all alive at once), but the C++ programs differ in structure: Asio builds a vector of N lazily-started awaitables and then co_spawns each on one io_context thread; concurrencpp copies two shared_ptrs into every coroutine frame and uses one worker_thread_executor plus its timer_queue; tokio spawns each task on the default multi-thread runtime and keeps the JoinHandles. Tokio is the largest at 1 task (3,092 KB vs Asio 1,668 KB) and only pulls ahead from 10k tasks. Libunifex hangs at 100k and 1M. The tokio repo itself makes no comparison to C++ runtimes.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Rust async/await versus C++20 coroutines performance evaluation paper benchmark throughput' surfaced Xavorim/cpp_tasks_bench.

verification.tier_reason: Xavorim/cpp_tasks_bench README lists the exact peak-RSS figures (/usr/bin/time) for tokio, concurrencpp, Asio and libunifex at 1, 10k, 100k and 1M tasks on an i7-8550U under WSL; code is public (asio_bench/main.cpp, concurrencpp_bench/main.cpp, tokio_bench/src/main.rs) and CMakeLists.txt fixes Release and cargo --release, but the C++ compiler is not named and the C++ libraries are unpinned, so not A; a 4-star one-person repo is not a well-known independent suite, so C.
verification.notes: Confirm at C: numbers match the benchmark README exactly (1M tasks: tokio 214,136 KB vs concurrencpp 605,972 KB and Asio 853,144 KB, about 2.8x and 4.0x less, derived); same -O3-equivalent Release builds per CMakeLists.txt; tokio metadata (MIT, 33.4k stars, last commit 2026-10-11) checks out. Shortcomings to record: one-person 2023 hobby benchmark, compiler unnamed, unpinned C++ library versions, memory-only single-run figures on WSL, tokio larger at 1 task, library-level not language-level claim.

corrected_fields.compiler_and_flags: C++20 with coroutines, compiler not named, CMake Release default, no flags listed; Rust build via cargo (profile unstated)

The README says the original article's methodology was criticised and the author replicated it anyway. name: Embassy (async Rust executor) vs FreeRTOS
baseline: FreeRTOS (C RTOS, used through the CMSIS-RTOS v2 wrapper in an STM32CubeIDE project) on an STM32F446ZE
workload: Same toy firmware on a NUCLEO-F446ZE at 180 MHz in Embassy, RTIC and FreeRTOS (CMSIS-RTOS v2 over ST HAL): one task blinks an LED every 100 ms, a button task waits on the EXTI13 user-button interrupt and toggles GPIO PG1 (interrupt-to-task latency read on an oscilloscope), formats a 32-byte message and queues it to a UART writer task. Per search-result summaries (blog unreachable), the post compares interrupt latency, program size, static RAM and ease of programming.
claimed_speedup: README quote: 'It obsoletes the need for a traditional RTOS with kernel context switching, and is faster and smaller than one!' No figures appear on any page that was opened; the blog post that carries them (tweedegolf.nl, async-rust-vs-rtos-showdown) could not be reached from this environment.
compiler_and_flags: Rust (rust/Cargo.toml): nightly toolchain (feature type_alias_impl_trait), [profile.release] opt-level = 3, lto = true, codegen-units = 1, incremental = false, debug = true (debug info only), embassy and embassy-stm32 from git master of early 2022. C (c/.cproject, STM32CubeIDE 1.8.0, MCU ARM GCC arm-none-eabi-): Release configuration C optimization -O3 with -g0 and no LTO (C++ option -Os, unused by this C project); the Debug configuration leaves the optimization level at the IDE default. The repo does not say which C configuration was measured, and no compiler versions are stated for either side.
hardware: STM32F446ZE (Arm Cortex-M4F) on NUCLEO-F446ZE
stars_or_usage: embassy-rs/embassy: 9.9k stars, 1.7k forks; tweedegolf/async-rtos-showdown: 18 stars, 2 forks, 3 commits (2022-01-04 to 2022-02-17)
tradeoffs: Cooperative async tasks, not preemptive threads: a task that does not yield blocks the others, and priorities work through multiple executors/interrupts. Needs Rust nightly features in the 2022 snapshot; no C++ API.
caveats: Tier D because no number could be read from any opened page; the blog post with the figures (tweedegolf.nl/en/blog/65/async-rust-vs-rtos-showdown) was unreachable (DNS ENOTFOUND), as were the zeli.app and hn.svelte.dev mirrors. Secondary search summaries (snippet only) say Embassy used less RAM and flash but FreeRTOS had better interrupt latency, so 'faster' is not established; Reddit r/embedded and Hacker News commenters said worst-case latency was not measured, only the standard deviation, and flagged the C app's static RAM figure. The verifier read the C side and found it does not do the same work as the Rust side: (1) the UART writer uses blocking polled HAL_UART_Transmit, while Embassy writes over DMA asynchronously; (2) the C message formatting uses newlib snprintf (configUSE_NEWLIB_REENTRANT 1), while Rust uses core::fmt into an ArrayString; (3) the C button task's 'only react to falling edges' block sets the same RTSR/FTSR bits as the rising-edge block (EXTI->RTSR |= pin; EXTI->FTSR &= ~pin), so the C firmware waits on two rising edges and never on a falling edge; (4) the EXTI path goes through the ST HAL callback and the CMSIS-RTOS v2 wrapper (osThreadFlagsSet) instead of native FreeRTOS calls. FreeRTOSConfig.h is the untuned CubeMX default: a static 15360-byte heap (configTOTAL_HEAP_SIZE), three 512-byte task stacks, trace facility, software timers, recursive mutexes and generic task selection (configUSE_PORT_OPTIMISED_TASK_SELECTION 0) all on, which inflates the C side's static RAM and flash. Build settings are not equivalent: the Rust side uses LTO and codegen-units = 1 at opt-level 3, the C Release build -O3 without LTO (larger code than -Os), and the repo does not say whether the Debug or Release C build was measured. The showdown repo is a Feb 2022 snapshot built on Embassy master of that date, so the result predates four years of Embassy and FreeRTOS changes. A cooperative executor versus a preemptive RTOS is not a like-for-like scheduling comparison. The only claim in the embassy repo itself is a README sentence linking the blog.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Embassy async rust vs FreeRTOS benchmark latency context switch'; opened github.com/embassy-rs/embassy README, github.com/tweedegolf/async-rtos-showdown (README, rust/Cargo.toml, c/.cproject, commits).
why_faster: README: async tasks compile into cooperatively scheduled state machines that share one stack, need no per-task stack sizing and no dynamic allocation, so no kernel context switch is paid.

verification.tier_reason: The benchmark repo (tweedegolf/async-rtos-showdown) holds the Embassy (rust/), RTIC (rtic/) and FreeRTOS (c/) firmware, but neither it nor the Embassy README carries a single number; the figures exist only in the tweedegolf.nl blog post, which is unreachable here (DNS ENOTFOUND), and two WebSearch passes returned no figures even in snippets, so the entry stays at D.
verification.notes: Confirm at D: Embassy is notable (9.9k stars) and the comparison code is public, but no numbers were reachable and secondary summaries say FreeRTOS won interrupt latency. Shortcomings to record: no numbers reachable (blog blocked); C baseline is untuned CubeMX FreeRTOS behind the CMSIS-RTOS v2 wrapper and ST HAL with a 15 KB static heap, blocking polled UART vs Embassy DMA, newlib snprintf vs core::fmt, a falling-edge EXTI configuration bug, and no LTO on the C side against LTO plus codegen-units = 1 on the Rust side; worst-case latency not measured; 2022 snapshot. If the blog is ever reached, the tier could rise only to C or B, not A, because the C and Rust firmware do different work and the measured C configuration and compiler versions are unstated.

name: CBQN (BQN array language) - CRLF-to-LF conversion versus plain C
language: BQN (implementation in C, SIMD kernels generated with Singeli)
baseline: Plain scalar C loop for the same line-ending conversion (crlf_to_lf), compiled with clang 15.0.7 -O3 -march=native
workload: Replace every CRLF with LF in a byte buffer of 100 to 1,000,000 bytes with a CRLF about every 100 characters; BQN one-liner (cr!=) with (0 shifted lf!=) filtered by Replicate versus a scalar C loop; the page also reports selection and compiler benchmarks.
claimed_speedup: Page text: BQN breaks even with C at a little under 200 bytes and hits 5x C's speed on inputs of a few thousand bytes or more with AVX-512 disabled, over 10x with AVX-512 until cache becomes a bottleneck. Page timings on a Tiger Lake i5-1135G7 (a CRLF every ~100 bytes): C (clang 15.0.7 -O3 -march=native) 0.555 ns/elt from 10k to 1M bytes (0.613 at 100 bytes); CBQN avx2/bmi2/pclmul build 0.893 (100 bytes, slower than C), 0.127 (3k), 0.106 (10k), 0.094 (30k), 0.107 (1M) ns/elt, about 4.4x at 3k and 5.2-5.9x from 10k up (derived from page data); CBQN native build (AVX-512) 0.0526 (10k), 0.0506 (30k), 0.0537 (100k), 0.0787 (1M) ns/elt, about 10.3-11.0x from 10k to 300k and 7.1x at 1M (derived from page data). The page's selection figures (0.04 ns per selection from a table of 32 or fewer 1-byte values via shuffles versus 0.2 ns via gather) are two CBQN code paths, not a C measurement. The compiler benchmark (implementation/bootbench.md) is a separate claim: boot3.bqn in CBQN compiles boot2.bqn in 270.6 us versus 415.5 us for dzaima's comp.c built with clang 15.0 (system values and error handling removed), average of 10,000 runs on a Skylake i5-6200U, i.e. 35% less time (about 1.54x, derived from page data); the two compilers use different algorithms and the C build flags are not stated.
compiler_and_flags: C baseline: clang 15.0.7, 'clang -O3 -march=native lineending.c' (gcc 12.2.1 also discussed: branching code, slightly faster at low density, much slower at high). CBQN built at commit 0d2631a2 with FFI, singeli x86-64 avx2 bmi2 pclmul (and a native build)
hardware: Intel Tiger Lake Core i5-1135G7
why_faster: Array primitives are implemented with hand-written SIMD, lookup tables and blocked multi-pass techniques (Replicate compresses with AVX2/AVX-512 mask operations, adapts to sparse inputs), which compilers do not generate from a scalar branching loop (no SIMD scan, movmask or compress idioms from portable C). The page itself says this is a best case: 'Your BQN programs are unlikely to outperform equivalent C programs' and specialized C is always faster.
tradeoffs: Whole-array style only: per-primitive call overhead, benefits grow with array length (hundreds to thousands of elements) and small element types; poor for sequential, data-dependent loops, cryptography with wrapping integer ops, and C++-style object dispatch. Interpreter, so C interop is through an FFI with copying. Licensing is a per-file mix with timsort (MIT) and Ryu (Apache-2.0/Boost) exceptions.
caveats: First-party measurement by the BQN author on one machine; both programs, the C compile line and the CBQN commit and build options are on the page, so it is reproducible (CBQN builds at -O3 with the system cc by default; the compiler used for CBQN is not named). The C baseline is the plain portable scalar loop the author took from his 2017 Dyalog talk; clang 15 makes it branchless and unrolls it 4x, so it is not crippled, but no SIMD-intrinsic or memchr/memcpy-chunk C version was tested and the page says specialized C is always faster. The win is CBQN's hand-written Singeli SIMD Replicate primitive (an adaptive sparse/dense compress) against compiler output for a scalar loop: a best case for BQN primitives, as the page itself says ('combinations of primitives never do so well'); density 1/100 is described as not particularly favourable. Not the same algorithm in the strict sense (data-parallel mask plus Replicate versus a sequential scan), but output is identical. The selection figures (0.04 versus 0.2 ns) compare two CBQN paths, not C. The compiler benchmark side claim (35% faster) ran on different hardware (i5-6200U), compares different compiler designs and states no C flags. The page dates from 2023 (clang 15.0.7, gcc 12.2.1; 'the C compilers of today (2023)') and CBQN has changed since. Licence: most files LGPL-3.0-only OR GPL-3.0-only OR MPL-2.0 at the user's choice; timsort files MIT and Ryu Apache-2.0 or BSL-1.0.
found_via: github.com/mlochbaum/BQN docs/implementation listing, page 'Performance in BQN versus C' (versusc.html); CBQN README for licensing; no WebSearch used

name: TriangularSolve.jl
baseline: Intel MKL (libmkl_rt.so loaded through MKL.jl; MKL version not stated) triangular solve called through Julia LinearAlgebra: rdiv!(copyto!(C, A), UpperTriangular(B)) and the 3-argument ldiv!(C, LowerTriangular(B), A) on the Intel run. The M1 run prints no BLAS configuration or versioninfo, so its BLAS is not named.
workload: 100x100 Float64 triangular solves with 100 right-hand sides (rdiv! UpperTriangular, ldiv! LowerTriangular), median of 10000 samples, single and multi-threaded.

UpperTriangular 17.916 us vs MKL rdiv!(copyto!(C, A), UpperTriangular(B)) 19.852 us (1.11x, derived from page data); ldiv! LowerTriangular 19.694 us vs MKL ldiv!(C, LowerTriangular(B), A) 21.561 us (1.09x, derived from page data). Multithreaded (JULIA_NUM_THREADS=8; the README sets MKL to min(Threads.nthreads(), num_cores()) threads, which is 4 on this 4-core/8-thread CPU): rdiv! 8.769 us vs 14.163 us (1.62x, derived from page data); ldiv! 9.871 us vs 15.258 us (1.55x, derived from page data). Apple M1 single thread, BLAS not named: rdiv! 21.624 us vs 46.166 us (2.13x, derived from page data); ldiv! 34.375 us vs 49.124 us (1.43x, derived from page data), and a second ldiv! run of 23.875 us against the same 49.124 us baseline (2.06x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.8.0-DEV.438 (commit 88a6376e99, 2021-08-28), libLLVM 12.0.1 ORCJIT with tigerlake target, JULIA_NUM_THREADS=8, no julia command-line options stated (Julia JIT, no compile flags). BLAS.set_num_threads(1) for the single-thread rows and BLAS.set_num_threads(min(Threads.nthreads(), num_cores())) for the multithreaded rows. MKL, MKL.jl and TriangularSolve versions not stated. The M1 run gives no Julia version or versioninfo.
hardware: 11th Gen Intel Core i7-1165G7 @ 2.80GHz (Linux); Apple M1 Mac (single-threaded only).
stars_or_usage: 12 stars; part of the JuliaSIMD/LoopVectorization ecosystem
tradeoffs: Only Float32/Float64 with at least two right-hand sides, and the README says only rdiv! with UpperTriangular and ldiv! with LowerTriangular are the supported configurations on the benchmarked paths; vector right-hand sides use pure-Julia sweeps.
caveats: Single matrix size (N=100) from a 2021 author REPL session on a Julia 1.8 development build, on a package version that has since been substantially rewritten (August 2026 kernel changes: native left-upper/right-lower kernels, shortened backward-substitution chains, inlined backward panel kernels), with no re-run; the README still ends with a stale line saying only rdiv!/UpperTriangular and ldiv!/LowerTriangular are supported. The baseline is closed-source, hand-tuned MKL (not a C/C++ -O3 build of the same algorithm), its version is not stated, and the M1 rows compare against an unnamed BLAS with no versioninfo. The single-thread Intel advantage is only about 9-11%; the larger multithreaded and M1 gaps are where small-size threading and call overhead matter most. The README's copy-paste script calls BLAS.set_num_threads(Threads.nthreads()) before the single-thread pair, unlike the REPL session it reproduces. The README gives no mechanism, and the baseline timings include LinearAlgebra's copy of A into C, which is equal work because TriangularSolve's 3-argument form also writes out of place. Not a language-level claim: TriangularSolve is a pure-Julia library (no BLAS call in the matrix path) that beats one vendor library at one small size. Source comments claim the vector right-hand-side path beats BLAS trsv by up to 7x below n=256, but no published harness backs that.

name: D (gdc, ldc2) matmul with std.numeric.dotProduct in kostya/benchmarks
baseline: C/gcc 16.1.0 and C/clang 22.1.8 (-O3 -march=native -flto=auto, -std=c23) transposed dot-product matmul of 1500x1500 doubles
workload: Allocate, generate and multiply two 1500x1500 double matrices; the D version transposes b and calls std.numeric.dotProduct per output cell, the C version transposes b and runs one scalar accumulation loop.
claimed_speedup: kostya/benchmarks matmul table (median, Xeon E-2324G, README updated 2026-07-19): D/gdc 1.505 s, D/ldc2 1.722 s, D/dmd 1.880 s versus C/gcc 3.034 s and C/clang 3.067 s, i.e. gdc about 2.0x, ldc2 about 1.76x and dmd about 1.61x faster than gcc C (derived from page data). Rust 3.067 s, Zig 3.071 s and Nim/gcc 3.091 s tie with C. Not like for like: the D program calls std.numeric.dotProduct (two partial sums) while every tied language runs the single-accumulator loop; in the like-for-like plb2 matmul (same i-k-j loop in D and C, Apple M1) D ldc2 1.35.0 takes 0.57 s versus C clang 15.0.0 0.54 s, so D is about 5% slower there (derived from page data). BLAS-backed rows (D lubeck 0.042 s, C++ Eigen 0.081 s, NumPy, Arraymancer) are library comparisons and excluded.
compiler_and_flags: From common/commands.mk: C gcc 16.1.0 / clang 22.1.8 '-Wall -Wextra -pedantic -Wcast-align -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries -std=c23'; D ldc2 1.41.0 '-O5 -release -boundscheck=off', gdc 14.2.0 '-O3 -frelease -finline -fbounds-check=off', dmd v2.111.0 '-O -release -inline -boundscheck=off'. The D builds carry no -march=native and no LTO, so the flag difference favours C.
hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) E-2324G, Debian forky/sid Docker image, README updated 2026-07-19
why_faster: Derived by the searcher from the source, not stated by the suite: Phobos std.numeric.dotProduct (std/numeric.d) unrolls 16-wide with two partial sums (sum0, sum1), a different floating-point reduction order; the C loop keeps one strict-FP accumulator and is built without -ffast-math, so the compiler cannot reassociate or vectorize it.
tradeoffs: Gain comes from one standard-library kernel, so a C programmer can match it by writing two or more accumulators or using -ffast-math; D's runtime and GC are not involved in the timed loop.
caveats: Not a language or compiler advantage: the high-level algorithm (transpose plus dot products) is the same, but the timed D path is Phobos' hand-unrolled two-accumulator dotProduct against a naive single-accumulator C loop, so summation order and results differ in the last bits (the harness only checks within 0.1 at n=101). Like for like (plb2, same loop in both languages) D ldc2 is slower than C. The C row is deliberately plain ('written as the average developer would'); C gets -march=native and -flto=auto that the D builds lack. gcc 16.1 and clang 22 are newer than the GCC 14 and LLVM bases of gdc and ldc2. Time includes allocation (D uses GC-allocated jagged arrays, C malloc/calloc rows) and matrix generation.

name: Fortran (gfortran) matmul in plb2
baseline: C (clang 15.0.0, make flags -O3 -fwrapv -flto) 1500x1500 double matmul with the same i-k-j loop order using double** rows
workload: Multiply two 1500x1500 double-precision matrices with triple-nested loops (no BLAS), one of four plb2 tasks. C (src/c/matmul.c) uses row pointers into one contiguous calloc block with i-k-j order (inner loop over j, c[i][j] += a[i][k] * b[k][j]); Fortran (src/fortran/matmul.F90) uses column-major explicit-shape dummy arrays with j-k-i order (inner loop over i), the same unit-stride access pattern and the same work. Elapsed wall time includes matrix generation and process startup.
claimed_speedup: matmul elapsed seconds on Apple M1: Fortran gfortran 13.2.0 0.51 s versus C clang 15.0.0 0.54 s, about 6% faster (derived from page data). Other compiled languages on the same row: Rust 0.56, Zig 0.56, Nim 0.56, Swift 0.56, D ldc2 0.57, V 0.57, Julia 0.76, Mojo 1.12. Fortran is the only language in the table that beats C on matmul.
compiler_and_flags: Fortran: gfortran 13.2.0 with FFLAGS=-O3 (src/fortran/Makefile); C: clang 15.0.0 via $(CC) with CFLAGS=-O3 -fwrapv -flto (src/c/Makefile). Neither side passes -march/-mcpu.
hardware: Apple M1 MacBook Pro (elapsed time, hyperfine)
why_faster: Not stated by the source. Searcher inference only: Fortran dummy arguments may not alias and arrays are contiguous, so gfortran can vectorize the inner loop without alias checks, whereas the C version indexes through double** rows.
tradeoffs: CC0 dedication (no patent grant). Fortran version needs gfortran; plb2 measures a naive triple loop, not tuned BLAS-level matmul.
caveats: Margin is about 6% (0.51 s versus 0.54 s) on one machine, single figures without variance in the table, and the rows were timed on different days (Fortran timing added 2024-01-04 as plb2 grew through January 2024), so this is a near-tie that may sit within run-to-run noise. Different compiler backends (gfortran versus clang), so the language and the compiler are confounded; no gcc-built C row exists. Both sides are at -O3 and neither uses -march; the C side adds -fwrapv and -flto (no effect expected on a one-file program). Fortran is the only language in the table that beats C on matmul; the README notes Clang already hoists the inner-loop invariants that many other languages cannot. Elapsed wall time includes process startup. CC0-1.0 dedication: no patent grant. Repository last changed 2025-01-30.

name: Halide
baseline: Expert hand-tuned C++ (OpenMP + Intel IPP), ARM NEON intrinsics/assembly and CUDA implementations of the same image-processing pipelines used as baselines in the PLDI 2013 paper (local Laplacian filters, bilateral grid, camera pipe, etc.)
workload: Image-processing pipelines written once as an algorithm plus a separate schedule (tiling, fusion, vectorization, parallelism): local Laplacian filters (99 stages) and bilateral grid on quad-core x86, plus camera raw pipe and others on ARM/CUDA, versus the hand-tuned expert code for the same pipelines.
claimed_speedup: PLDI 2013 abstract (search snippet only): Halide programs written in a few hours, with schedules found by stochastic search (autotuning), run up to 5x faster than hand-tuned C, intrinsics and CUDA implementations that experts optimized over weeks or months. Results-table fragments (snippet only; rows could not be matched to applications): '3.7x shorter / 2.1x faster' and '3x shorter / 5.9x faster', against baselines labelled Tuned C++, C++ OpenMP+IPP and hand-written CUDA on a quad-core x86 and a CUDA GPU. Pairing 2.1x with local Laplacian (262-line C++/OpenMP+IPP against 62 algorithm and 7 schedule lines, 335 ms vs 158 ms) and 5.9x with bilateral grid is the search agent's inference and is unconfirmed.
hardware: Quad-core x86 desktop, ARM and CUDA GPU platforms (exact CPU models not confirmed; paper PDF could not be opened)
why_faster: Decouples the algorithm from its schedule: the programmer or autoscheduler explores loop tiling, producer-consumer fusion, recomputation vs storage, vectorization and parallelism without rewriting the algorithm, which finds locality/parallelism trade-offs that were too laborious to hand-code in C++.
tradeoffs: Embedded DSL: requires writing a Halide pipeline and a schedule (C++17 API or Python bindings), ahead-of-time or JIT compiled through LLVM; schedule quality depends on the expert or autoscheduler; image/array pipelines only, not general code. LICENSE.txt is MIT with apps/bgu under Apache-2.0.
caveats: Numbers come only from WebSearch snippets of the PLDI 2013 paper (Ragan-Kelley et al.; the PDF hosts are blocked here, so the table was never opened); the snippet tool said the table text was garbled, so the row attributions (2.1x local Laplacian, 5.9x bilateral grid) are inferred, and the 5.9x row exceeds the abstract's 'up to 5x' without explanation. The baselines are the authors' 2012-13 expert implementations on 2012 hardware with CPU models, compilers and flags unconfirmed. The local Laplacian baseline calls Intel IPP library routines, so part of that comparison is Halide against a vendor library rather than against hand-written C++. The algorithm is the same mathematical pipeline on both sides, but the win comes from a different loop organization (fusion, tiling, recomputation, vectorization and parallelism chosen by the schedule and an autotuner), not from better code generation for the same loop nest. The repo does not carry the paper's baselines or harness; apps/blur/test.cpp does time naive C++, hand-written SSE intrinsics (blur_fast) and Halide side by side but publishes no numbers (enrichment lead). Halide is a C++-embedded DSL compiled through LLVM, so pipelines are callable directly from C++. License is MIT for the core; apps/bgu is Apache-2.0 (both OSI).

name: Bessels.jl
baseline: SpecialFunctions.jl wrappers: openlibm (C, FreeBSD msun) j0/y0/j1/y1/jn/yn for integer-order and order-0 and 1 calls, AMOS zbes* routines (Fortran, via openspecfun) for non-integer order, so only the order-0 and order-1 rows have a C baseline
workload: Float64 evaluation of Bessel J, Y, I, K functions and gamma for random x and order nu between 0 and 100.
claimed_speedup: README Benchmarks (relative speed increase over SpecialFunctions.jl): besselj0 2.5x, bessely0 2.3x (the two rows whose baseline is openlibm C), besselj(nu,x) 6x, bessely(nu,x) 5x, besseli0 10x, besseli(nu,x) 7x, besselk0 10x, besselk(nu,x) 4x, Bessels.gamma 5x. README prose: 'in general 5-10x faster'.
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.7.2 (no C/Fortran flags: baselines are prebuilt binary libraries)
hardware: Apple M1 run under Rosetta (x86 emulation)
why_faster: Different algorithms: piecewise polynomial/rational approximations per domain written in pure Julia that inline and vectorize, versus AMOS general-order series/recurrences and libm's older rational approximations.
tradeoffs: README admits accuracy is sometimes 'within a digit or two' of the baselines rather than better (its own error table vs ArbNumerics gives mean/max relative errors such as besselj0 3e-16/6e-14 and besselj(5.0,x) 3e-14/2e-11); positive real arguments mainly, limited complex support; Float64 focus.
caveats: First-party, run under Rosetta emulation, no compiler flags or CPU model beyond 'Apple M1', and speedups are ratios with no absolute times. The comparison harness is not in the repo: benchmark/benchmark.jl times only Bessels functions (no SpecialFunctions.jl calls), and its 'bessely' group actually times besselj0/besselj1. Most of the baseline is Fortran AMOS reached through SpecialFunctions' complex-argument path (besseli, besselk and non-integer besselj/bessely all call zbes* via openspecfun), and a Fortran-vs-Julia comparison is outside this catalogue's scope; only besselj0/bessely0 (2.5x, 2.3x) are measured against C code (openlibm j0/y0, which openlibm's Make.inc builds at -O3 by default), and that baseline goes through non-inlinable Julia ccall wrappers. claimed_speedup: README Performance (million cycles, ispc build vs serial C++ build; the README's own ratios): grav3Daccel 6.79x (i5-2467M, AVX, n=10000), 8.01x (Xeon E5-2640, AVX, n=20000), 14.03x (i7-5960X, AVX2, n=50000); vortex3Dvel 7.06x, 8.15x, 10.95x. vortex3Dvel_mt1d (ispc SIMD plus ispc tasks across all cores, against the single-threaded serial vortex3Dvel time) 12.45x, 86.49x, 88.10x. These rows compare a multithreaded build with one scalar thread and are not like for like.

Timing: rdtsc million cycles via timing.h (from ispc); minimum of 4 ispc runs and 2 serial runs by default (nbody.cpp).
hardware: 2-core i5-2467M 2.0/2.3GHz (Fedora 21); 6-core Xeon E5-2640 2.5GHz (RHEL 6.5); 8-core i7-5960X 4.5GHz OC (Fedora 21).
tradeoffs: GPL-2.0 licensed (copyleft); needs the ispc toolchain; structure-of-arrays data layout; single-step O(N^2) kernels only, no tree codes.
caveats: The C++ baseline is not an -O3 equivalent of the ispc build. common.mk builds it at -O2 with no -march (generic x86-64, SSE2) and no -ffast-math, while ispc gets explicit AVX/AVX2 targets. The serial loop accumulates in strict sequential order through pointers into the output arrays (tax[i] etc., all float* that may alias the inputs), so clang cannot vectorise it; the ispc version accumulates into lane-private partial sums and calls reduce_add once per target. The unsuffixed literals 0.01 (grav3Daccel) and 1.0 (vortex3Dvel, giving a double-precision divide) promote every C++ interaction to double, whereas ispc treats such literals as float (ispc docs). With the pre-GCC-6 libstdc++ headers of the 2015 systems, sqrt(float) from <math.h> probably also resolved to double sqrt (inference). The mt1d rows add multithreading against one scalar thread. Results are compared only by printing two sample particles; there is no automated check. One run set per machine, cycles not wall time, n differs per machine, 2015-2017 compilers and CPUs, and no ARM numbers despite NEON targets. timing.h, tasksys.cpp and the makefile scheme come from the ispc examples, so this is the same serial-vs-ispc evidence type as the ispc/ispc entry.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/ispc listing
why_faster: Same kernel source compiled by ispc for SIMD (SSE2/SSE4/AVX/AVX2/FMA3) with runtime dispatch, versus the serial x87 build.

verification.tier_reason: The README Performance section gives serial and ispc mcycles on three named CPUs with clang 3.5.0/3.4.2. The harness (grav3Daccel/nbody.cpp, nbody_serial.cpp, nbody.ispc) and flags (common.mk: clang++ -O2 -m64; ispc -O2 with sse2/sse4/avx1/avx2 targets) are public. But the ispc version is unstated and the C++ side is not an equivalent build (-O2, no -march, strict FP, double-precision literals, sequential accumulator), so it cannot be A. First-party, so C; D is arguable for the mt1d rows (threads versus one scalar thread).
verification.notes: Numbers and ratios match the README exactly; metadata (GPL-2.0, 5 stars, 1 fork, 26 commits, last commit 2017-03-21, abandoned) checks out. Corrected compiler_and_flags (the -O2 flags are in common.mk, not unstated), the 'x87' baseline wording, and same_algorithm to false (lane-private partial sums vs a sequential accumulator, plus C++ double literals). Kept at C under the kostya Julia matmul precedent (release C build, unequal FP semantics); D is arguable since the C++ build lacks -march and does double-precision work. The mt1d 86-88x rows are threads versus one thread. It overlaps the wave-13 ispc/ispc entry (same compiler, same serial-vs-ispc harness code taken from ispc's examples), so the orchestrator may record duplicate. Shortcomings to record: -O2 generic-ISA strict-FP C++ baseline, double-precision literals in the C++ kernels, mt1d rows compare threads with one thread, no correctness check, 2015-2017 toolchain, cycles only.

name: Futhark
baseline: Hand-written OpenCL reference implementations from Rodinia 3.1 (CUDA for Myocyte on NVIDIA), Parboil 2.5 (MRI-Q) and FinPar (LocVolCalib, OptionPricing); the four Accelerate benchmarks (Crystal, Fluid, Mandelbrot, N-body) were compared against Accelerate 0.15.1 (a Haskell DSL with a CUDA backend), not C/C++.
workload: 16 GPU benchmarks manually translated to Futhark (Rodinia Backprop, CFD, HotSpot, K-means, LavaMD, Myocyte, NN, Pathfinder, SRAD; FinPar LocVolCalib, OptionPricing; Parboil MRI-Q; Accelerate Crystal, Fluid, Mandelbrot, N-body), datasets in the paper's Table 2; runtime averaged over 10 runs, excluding input upload, result readback and OpenCL context creation and kernel build on both sides (Rodinia timing patched to match).
claimed_speedup: PLDI 2017 paper: from about 0.6x (slower, FinPar LocVolCalib on AMD W8100) to 16x (Rodinia NN on GTX 780 Ti) against hand-written OpenCL/CUDA reference implementations; geometric mean 1.81x over the 12 benchmarks that have a low-level CUDA/OpenCL implementation; Futhark slower on 4 of those 12 (geometric mean 0.79x on them). Table 1 runtimes on GTX 780 Ti, reference vs Futhark in ms: NN 178.9 vs 11.0, Backprop 46.9 vs 20.7, K-means 1597.7 vs 572.2, Myocyte 2733.6 vs 555.4 (CUDA reference), Pathfinder 18.4 vs 7.4, SRAD 19.9 vs 16.1, MRI-Q 20.2 vs 15.5, OptionPricing 136.0 vs 106.8; slower: CFD 1878.2 vs 2235.9, HotSpot 35.9 vs 45.3, LavaMD 5.1 vs 6.7, LocVolCalib 1211.1 vs 1293.2. Artifact W8100 speedup files: srad 5.60, nn 5.14, hotspot 3.58, backprop 3.21, pathfinder 2.77, lavaMD 1.25, mri-q 1.24, OptionPricing 1.19, cfd 0.86, kmeans 0.79, LocVolCalib 0.62.
compiler_and_flags: Futhark compiler git 78c956ba58057ca6773cefb466efef2fa65c1386 with the OpenCL backend and no benchmark-specific flags; references built by their own suite Makefiles with gcc/g++ (-lOpenCL) and nvcc (CUDA 8.0 on NVIDIA). The paper and artifact state no host compiler versions or optimisation flags; Rodinia OpenCL Makefiles in the yuhc/gpu-rodinia mirror use g++ -g -O2 (backprop) and -g -O3 (nn). GPU kernels on both sides are compiled by the vendor OpenCL driver.
hardware: NVIDIA GeForce GTX 780 Ti with CUDA 8.0 and AMD FirePro W8100 (OpenCL benchmarks only); host CPU not stated.
stars_or_usage: 2.8k stars, 210 forks; futhark-benchmarks 48 stars; futhark-pldi17 artifact 8 stars
tradeoffs: Purely functional ML-family language; programs are rewritten in Futhark and called from C, Python or other hosts through generated code; sequential/irregular code does not fit.
caveats: The wins are mostly not a language-level effect: the paper attributes them to the hand-written references leaving work unoptimised, namely Rodinia NN leaving 100 reduce operations sequential on the CPU, Backprop leaving a reduction sequential, K-means not parallelising the cluster-centre update, and Myocyte/MRI-Q lacking coalescing or locality optimisation; the authors say the 0.79x geometric mean on the 4 slower benchmarks is 'a better estimation of where Futhark stands in relation to hand-optimised GPU code'. HotSpot and Pathfinder references use time tiling that Futhark lacks. Same benchmarks but different parallelisation strategies, so same_algorithm is false for the large speedups (NN 16x, Backprop, K-means, Myocyte). Accelerate rows compare against a Haskell DSL, not C. Timings exclude transfer and kernel build on both sides. Numbers are from 2017 Futhark on 2013-2014 GPUs; the C and multicore CPU backends are not compared against C here, and futhark-benchmarks itself publishes no results. futhark-website performance.md compares against Thrust and Rodinia HotSpot only as graphs, without numbers or hardware in the text. A 2026 arXiv snippet (seen only by the search agent) reports big-integer multiplication about 1.35x slower than hand-coded CUDA. Paper PDF: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/diku-dk/futhark-website/HEAD/publications/pldi17.pdf.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/futhark; github.com/orgs/diku-dk/repositories

verification.tier_reason: Upgraded from D: the peer-reviewed PLDI 2017 paper (Henriksen et al., PDF checked into diku-dk/futhark-website publications/pldi17.pdf) reports Table 1 runtimes and Figure 13 speedups against hand-written OpenCL/CUDA references from Rodinia 3.1, Parboil and FinPar on an NVIDIA GTX 780 Ti (CUDA 8.0) and an AMD FirePro W8100, and the public artifact repo diku-dk/futhark-pldi17 (Makefile, Rodinia instrumentation patch, paper_data/aux_runtimes matching the W8100 column) reproduces it. Not A: host compiler versions, flags, OpenCL driver versions and host CPU are not stated.
verification.notes: Tier upgraded from D to B: the PLDI 2017 paper and its artifact were reachable via GitHub (futhark-website/publications/pldi17.pdf; diku-dk/futhark-pldi17 paper_data/aux_runtimes matches the paper's W8100 column). Main shortcoming for the orchestrator: the large speedups come from under-optimised Rodinia references (sequential CPU reductions in NN and Backprop, an unparallelised K-means update), and the authors themselves estimate 0.79x against hand-optimised GPU code, so same_algorithm is false and this is not a language win; consider whether the NN and Backprop rows fall under the crippled-baseline precedent. Metadata confirmed: ISC licence, last commit 2026-10-11 ('This is 0.28.1'), not archived, not a fork.

A web search snippet of a 2026 arXiv paper reports Futhark big-integer multiplication about 1.35x slower than hand-coded CUDA, i.e. parity-or-slower, not faster. name: C# (Staged) on .NET: Brainfuck bench.b in kostya/benchmarks
baseline: C++/g++ brainfuck (brainfuck/bf.cpp): an AST-walking interpreter with std::vector ops, g++ -O3 -march=native -flto
workload: Run the bench.b Brainfuck program; the staged C# version builds a closed generic type per Brainfuck program (static abstract interface members, ref structs) and lets RyuJIT compile it, inside the timed region.
claimed_speedup: bench.b: C# (Staged)/.NET Core 0.373 s (36.62 + 0.25 MiB, 14.33 J) vs C++/g++ 1.097 s (3.38 MiB, 46.21 J), C/gcc 1.112 s, C/clang 1.136 s, C++/clang++ 1.167 s (about 2.9x vs g++, derived from page data). The non-staged C#/.NET Core interpreter takes 1.280 s, slower than C++/g++.
compiler_and_flags: C++ baseline: g++ 16.1.0 -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries -std=c++23 (common/commands.mk GCC_CPP_BUILD); clang++ 22.1.8 row uses the same flags plus -stdlib=libc++; C rows -std=c23. C# (Staged): .NET 10.0.100, dotnet build -c Release, root Directory.Build.props sets TieredCompilation=false (every method JIT-compiled once at full optimisation, no tier-0 or dynamic PGO), ServerGarbageCollection=true, ConcurrentGarbageCollection=true; RyuJIT targets the host CPU at run time.
hardware: Intel Xeon E-2324G (README Environment section); Debian forky/sid Docker image
tradeoffs: Run-time compile inside the process: needs the .NET JIT and about 36 MiB resident versus about 3.4 MiB for the C++ interpreter; wins only for programs long enough to amortize compilation.
caveats: Different algorithm: the C++ baseline (brainfuck/bf.cpp) interprets a vector<Op> AST instruction by instruction, as brainfuck/README.md requires of every implementation ('interprets all bf instructions, one by one, without any squash or other hacks'), while the staged C# variant compiles the Brainfuck program to native code at run time (type construction and JIT inside the timed region), so it is listed as a separate '(Staged)' row. No C++ counterpart that also specializes on the program (template staging, LLVM ORC or asmjit, a BF-to-C compiler) was benchmarked, so the result shows runtime specialization beating an interpreter, not the .NET runtime beating C++ at the same work. The plain C# interpreter in the same suite is slower than C++/g++. The staged tape is a byte array with != 0 loop tests, the C++ tape a vector<int> with > 0 tests (outputs agree by checksum). The staged variant was contributed by hez2010 in PR #511 (merged 2025-11-17). It uses about 11x the memory of the C++ row (36.9 vs 3.38 MiB). Results are medians from one suite run on one machine (Xeon E-2324G), timed between libnotify start and stop messages, so process start-up is excluded for every language.
found_via: Suite-repo check after WebSearch for Julia/Java/.NET beating C++ returned only blog and forum threads; opened github.com/kostya/benchmarks README, brainfuck/ Makefile and staged sources via raw.githubusercontent.com.
why_faster: Runtime specialization on the input program (first Futamura-style staging): the JIT sees the whole Brainfuck program as types and removes interpretation overhead (derived from reading brainfuck/bf-staged.cs; the README gives no explanation).

verification.tier_reason: The measurement itself is reproducible (README bench.b table, brainfuck/bf-staged.cs vs brainfuck/bf.cpp, flags in common/commands.mk and Directory.Build.props, Xeon E-2324G), but the staged C# row runs a different algorithm (a run-time compiler) against the suite's C++ interpreter, so it cannot stand at A as a language-level win; capped at C like a tuned variant measured in place of the comparable program (Topaz precedent).
verification.notes: Numbers match the README row exactly; repo metadata (MIT, 2.9k stars, last commit 2026-07-19) checks out. Shortcoming: staged C# compiles the Brainfuck program at run time while the C++ baseline interprets it (the suite's brainfuck README requires interpretation), no C++ staged or JIT counterpart exists in the suite, and the plain C# interpreter is slower than C++ (1.280 vs 1.097 s); the win is runtime specialization, not the language. If the orchestrator reads the C++ interpreter as naive code against a tuned other-language version, the crippled-baseline precedent would put it at D.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: bench.b: C# (Staged)/.NET Core 0.373s vs C++/g++ 1.097s, C/gcc 1.112s, C++/clang++ 1.167s (about 2.9x vs g++, derived from page data); memory 36.6 MiB vs 3.38 MiB.
corrected_fields.compiler_and_flags: C++ baseline: g++ 16.1.0 -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries -std=c++23 (common/commands.mk); clang++ 22.1.8 row also present; runtimes: .NET 10.0.100, Scala 3.8.4, Racket 9.2

A C++ program that also compiled the Brainfuck program ahead of or at run time (template staging, JIT) was not benchmarked, so the result shows runtime specialization beats an interpreter, not that the language runtime is faster at the same algorithm. The non-staged versions in the same suite are slower than C++ (C#/.NET Core 1.280s vs C++/g++ 1.097s on bench.b). Single-suite, single-machine medians.

name: ClangJIT (Clang with JIT extensions for C++ templates)
baseline: The same Eigen expression (m = Ones + 0.00005*(m + m*m)) compiled ahead of time with runtime-sized Matrix<T,Dynamic,Dynamic> and float/double/long double dispatch, by the same Clang at -march=native -ffast-math -O3; the wiki also reports an AoT build specialized for one fixed size, which matches the JIT.
workload: Eigen bench/benchmark.cpp adapted: 40,000,000 repeats of small dense matrix operations; AoT runtime-sized matrices versus JIT-instantiated fixed-size matrices for sizes 3, 7 and 16, JIT compile time excluded from the runtime rows.
claimed_speedup: Runtime, double, 40,000,000 repeats, times reported by the code (JIT compile time excluded): size 3 JIT 1.0 s vs AoT dynamic-size 8.05 s vs AoT single fixed-size specialization 1.01 s; size 7 JIT 8.34 s vs AoT 20 s vs single specialization 8.45 s; size 16 JIT 35.3 s vs AoT 36.2 s vs single specialization 35.1 s (about 8x, 2.4x and 1.03x over dynamic-size AoT and parity with size-specialized AoT, derived from page data). Compile time (user): JIT only 3.5 s vs AoT double only 5.3 s and AoT float/double/long double with dispatch 9.7 s; one fixed-size specialization 2.95-4.95 s; includes and main only 2.58 s.
compiler_and_flags: ClangJIT (Clang fork, -fjit, [[clang::jit]] attribute) with -march=native -ffast-math -O3 on both sides per the wiki; the Clang used was built with GCC 8.2.0 in CMake RelWithDebInfo mode. Eigen version, ClangJIT commit and the benchmark's main() are not given.
hardware: Xeon E5-2699 (exact variant not stated)
tradeoffs: Needs a custom Clang/LLVM fork (not upstream); the program links the compiler infrastructure and compiles templates at run time (JIT start-up cost, memory, requires source or serialized AST available at run time); restrictions on decltype(auto), explicit specializations and pointer arguments listed on the wiki; the WG21 proposal P1609 for [[jit]] has not been adopted.
caveats: The run-time win is over Eigen's dynamic-size code path; the wiki's 'single specialization' AoT rows (1.01 s, 8.45 s, 35.1 s) equal the JIT rows, so JIT code is no faster than AoT C++ -O3 code that knows the size; the real advantage is lower compile time than instantiating many sizes or types ahead of time. JIT compile time is excluded from the runtime rows. First-party wiki, single runs without variance, CPU generation of the Xeon E5-2699 not stated, Eigen version not stated, main() omitted from the listings. The SC19 P3HPC paper (arXiv 1904.08555) was not reachable (arxiv.org, open-std.org P1609R0 and deepai blocked), so only the wiki was checked. Clang fork, last commit 2019-12-30. It is C++ with a JIT extension rather than another language, so it could also sit beside Easy::jit in wave 12 jits.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Clang-JIT C++ template instantiation at runtime speedup over ahead-of-time compiled code paper github' surfaced arXiv 1904.08555 and P1609; repo wiki then opened on github.com.
why_faster: Runtime values (matrix dimensions) become template arguments instantiated at run time, so the optimizer sees fixed sizes and can unroll and vectorize; only the sizes actually used are compiled (wiki: 'performance benefits of many AoT specializations, sometimes better, at a low compile-time cost').

verification.tier_reason: First-party wiki by the author with code listings for the timed functions, flags (-march=native -ffast-math -O3) and CPU family, but no main(), Eigen version, ClangJIT commit, CPU generation (E5-2699 v3 or v4) or run count, so not A; the peer-reviewed paper (arXiv 1904.08555, SC19 P3HPC workshop) could not be opened and its snippets give no numbers. The wiki's own size-specialized AoT rows match the JIT, so the win holds only against dynamic-size code.
verification.notes: Numbers match the wiki exactly; license Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception (llvm/LICENSE.TXT, legacy NCSA appended), 237 stars, 25 forks, last commit 2019-12-30 (abandoned) all check out. Shortcoming: the JIT beats only dynamic-size AoT Eigen; AoT code specialized to the same size ties it (1.01 vs 1.0 s, 8.45 vs 8.34 s, 35.1 vs 35.3 s), win shrinks to 1.03x at size 16, first-party wiki with partial methodology, paper unreachable. Not yet catalogued anywhere (wave 12 leads.md lists it as a lead); related to the wave 12 Easy::jit entry but not a duplicate.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: Runtime, 40M repeats, JIT compile time excluded: size 3 JIT 1.0s vs AoT 8.05s; size 7 JIT 8.34s vs AoT 20s; size 16 JIT 35.3s vs AoT 36.2s (about 8x, 2.4x and 1.03x, derived from page data). Compile time (user): JIT build 3.5s total vs AoT double-only 5.3s and AoT three-float-types-with-dispatch 9.7s.
corrected_fields.baseline: Ahead-of-time compiled Eigen benchmark (adapted bench/benchmark.cpp) using runtime-sized dynamic matrices, built with the same Clang at -O3 -march=native -ffast-math
corrected_fields.compiler_and_flags: ClangJIT (Clang fork, -fjit, [[clang::jit]] attribute) with -march=native -ffast-math -O3 as stated in the wiki table header; Clang itself built with GCC 8.2.0
corrected_fields.caveats: The AoT baseline is Eigen with dynamic (runtime-sized) matrices; the wiki's 'single specialization' column (1.01s, 8.45s, 35.1s) shows an AoT build specialized for one known size matches the JIT run time, so the win is over generic AoT code, not over size-specialized AoT code. Win shrinks to 1.03x at size 16. Wiki is first-party and numbers are single runs (no variance given). The paper (arXiv 1904.08555, SC19 P3HPC workshop) could not be opened (arxiv.org blocked), so only the wiki was checked. Whether the JIT'd code gets exactly the same -O3 level as the AoT code is assumed from the wiki's flag header. Repository last commit is Dec 2019.

name: OpenJDK HotSpot (Java 27) and GraalVM JIT: LangArena Etc::Words
baseline: C++ splitting with std::istringstream and counting in std::unordered_map<std::string,int> (g++ 16, clang++ 22); best C/C++ configuration is C++/G++/PGO at 1.587 s
workload: Split a large generated text into words and count word frequencies, then report the most frequent word.
claimed_speedup: Java/OpenJDK 1.272 s vs C++/G++ 1.638 s (prod, -O2), C++/G++ -O3 'Fast' 1.651 s, best of all 16 C/C++ configurations 1.587 s: about 1.25x faster than the best row and 1.29x faster than the prod row (derived from page data). Java on GraalVM JIT 1.15 s (1.4x faster than the best row); C#/JIT 1.422 s also wins; Julia 1.857 s does not.
compiler_and_flags: C/C++: Clang 22.1.8 (official LLVM release tarball; the clang_cpp container aliases g++ to clang++ and links the system libstdc++, no -stdlib=libc++) and GCC 16.0.1 20260322 (trunk, Ubuntu build), -std=c++20, glibc malloc. Headline 'prod' build (cpp/Makefile CXXFLAGS_PROD): -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer, linked with -Wl,-z,relro,-z,now -Wl,--gc-sections (not -O3). The same suite also builds 'Fast' (-O3 -march=native -mtune=native -pipe -fstack-protector -ftree-vectorize -funroll-loops), 'Unsafe' (-O3 -march=native -ffast-math -fno-stack-protector -fomit-frame-pointer -fvisibility=hidden -fno-trapping-math) and 'PGO' (-O2 plus -fprofile-instr-use or -fprofile-use) variants of every C and C++ benchmark; the Makefile passes -flto=thin (Fast) and -flto=full (Unsafe) only at the link step while the objects are compiled without -flto, so those builds probably get no LTO (inference from cpp/Makefile). All 16 Clang/GCC x C/C++ x prod/Fast/Unsafe/PGO configurations were compared here (instrumented PGO/Gen rows excluded). Managed side: Temurin OpenJDK 27+35 run as 'java -Xmx2g -jar' (default G1 GC, C2 JIT), GraalVM CE 25.4.4.1.1 (JDK 25.0.4.1.1) with -Xmx2g, dotnet 11.0.100-rc.1 (Release), Julia 1.13.1 with --threads=16 (versions and run commands from the results file).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X 8-Core Processor, 78GB RAM, x86_64 Linux (results file 2026-10-05, host kostya-ms7c37)
why_faster: Not stated by the suite. The C++ version tokenizes with istringstream operator>> and allocates std::string keys; the Java version uses String.split and HashMap (agent inference: library-level differences).
tradeoffs: Java peak RSS about 309 MB (GraalVM about 445 MB).
caveats: The win comes from the C++ tokenizer and per-node hash-map allocation, not from JIT compilation: C#/AOT and the AOT languages Rust, Crystal and Zig also beat every C++ row, so the 'runtime-jit-beats-aot' framing does not fit; a std::string_view split loop in C++ would likely change the result (inference, not measured). Both versions do the same work (whitespace split, hash count, max scan) over 50,000 words of 3-8 letters (all within libstdc++'s small-string buffer), 360 timed iterations. The C version (strdup of the whole text every iteration, strtok_r, uthash with strdup'd keys) is slower still at 1.963-2.084 s. Memory trade: Java/OpenJDK RSS 309 MB vs C++ 7.5-7.9 MB. Margin is modest (1.25x over the best C++ row, C++/G++/PGO 1.587 s) and rests on one run per configuration, although all 16 C/C++ configurations land between 1.587 and 2.042 s. LangArena's own README calls it 'a subjective benchmark', and the author says AI tools helped translate the tests between languages. benchmarks.rb runs each test once per configuration in its own process and records that single in-process timing (no repeats, no variance). Every language, C and C++ included, runs a warm-up of 20% of the iterations before the timer starts, so JIT compilation and startup are excluded. The headline C/C++ 'prod' rows are -O2 with hardening flags, but the -O3, PGO and fast-math variants were also measured and still lose on this test; the Makefile's LTO flags are link-only, so no configuration had real LTO. Rows were selected by the search agent as tests where a managed-runtime row beats every C/C++ row; most other tests in the suite go the other way (for example Sort::Quick, Sort::Merge and the Binarytrees::Arena variant). The per-benchmark ratios are derived from the results file, not stated by the suite.
found_via: GitHub: kostya/benchmarks README links to LangArena; parsed results/2026-10-05-kostya-ms7c37.js for tests where a Java, C# or Julia row is faster than every Clang/GCC C and C++ row

verification.tier_reason: Independent third-party suite with public code for both sides (cpp/src/words.cpp, java/src/main/java/benchmarks/Words.java), flags in cpp/Makefile and the results file's run-cmd entries, compiler and JVM versions and the CPU (AMD Ryzen 7 3800X) in results/2026-10-05-kostya-ms7c37.js; every number in the record matches the Etc::Words-runtime rows.
verification.notes: Numbers verified exactly (Java/OpenJDK 1.272 s, Java/GraalVM/JIT 1.15 s, C#/JIT 1.422 s, C++/G++ 1.638 s, C++/G++/Fast 1.651 s, C++/G++/PGO 1.587 s best, Julia 1.857 s). Shortcomings: the win is a standard-library effect (istringstream tokenizer plus node-per-key unordered_map against String.split and a GC'd HashMap), AOT C#, Rust, Crystal and Zig also beat C++, so the category label 'runtime-jit-beats-aot' misattributes it; single run per configuration; 40x more memory on the JVM; the Makefile's LTO flags are link-only.

corrected_fields.compiler_and_flags: C/C++: Clang 22.1.8 and GCC 16.0.1 20260322 (trunk). Headline 'prod' build is -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer (not -O3). The same suite also builds 'Fast' (-O3 -march=native -mtune=native -funroll-loops, thin LTO), 'Unsafe' (-O3 -march=native -ffast-math, full LTO) and 'PGO' (-O2 plus profile) variants of every C and C++ benchmark; all 16 Clang/GCC x C/C++ configurations were compared here. workload: 1500x1500 double matrix multiply (MSIZE 1500) written as plain loops (no BLAS) in each language.
claimed_speedup: Matmul (MSIZE 1500): Julia (no BLAS) 1.113s (MAD 0.017) vs C/gcc 3.034s (MAD 0.001) and C/clang 3.067s (about 2.7x vs C/gcc, derived from page data); energy 49.41 J vs 113.24 J. The other plain-loop rows (Rust 3.067s, Zig 3.071s, Go 3.153s, Java 3.057s) cluster with C. Library-backed rows (C++/g++ Eigen 0.081s, Julia with OpenBLAS threads: 1 0.170s) are a different algorithm class and are not the claim.
compiler_and_flags: C baseline: gcc 16.1.0 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic -Wcast-align -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries -std=c23 (common/commands.mk GCC_BUILD); the C/clang row uses clang 22.1.8 with the same flags (CLANG_BUILD). Julia run as julia --optimize=3 --check-bounds=no matmul.jl 1500 (common/commands.mk JULIA_RUN, matmul/Makefile run[matmul.jl]) with no -t flag; README Environment lists Julia v"1.11.6" while docker/Dockerfile at HEAD pins julia-1.12.6.
hardware: Intel Xeon E-2324G (README Environment section); Debian forky/sid Docker image

caveats: Not an equal-work, equal-optimisation comparison. The C inner loop is a scalar floating-point reduction (t += p[k] * r[k]) that gcc and clang at -O3 may not reorder or vectorise without -ffast-math, so it runs as one serial dependency chain; the Julia inner loop uses the other loop order (c[m,n] += a[m,k] * b[k,n] down a column-major column), whose iterations are independent and vectorise without reassociation, plus @simd ivdep (no alias checks), @fastmath (FMA contraction and reassociation allowed) and @inbounds. The C file is built with -std=c23, an ISO mode in which GCC's documented default is -ffp-contract=off, so the gcc build does not even fuse multiply-adds. A C version with the same loop order or with -ffast-math would likely close most of the gap. The Julia file wraps the outer loop in Threads.@threads, but neither JULIA_RUN nor docker/Dockerfile sets -t or JULIA_NUM_THREADS, so Julia's default of one thread applies (inferred from the build files, not stated on the README). The timed region includes matrix generation and allocation on both sides; Julia is warmed by calc(101) before timing, so JIT compilation of mul is outside the timed region. The README's Julia version (1.11.6) disagrees with the Dockerfile at HEAD (1.12.6), so the version behind the published row is uncertain. name: LuaJIT vs C and C++ hash-table word count (spion gist)
baseline: C (hand-written chained hash table, gcc -O3) and C++ (std::unordered_map<string,int> with a custom hash, g++ -O3 -std=gnu++0x)
workload: Count occurrences of the 19 words of a hard-coded, pre-split sentence over 1,000,000 passes in a string-keyed hash table, one lookup per word per pass. C: hand-written table of 256 buckets indexed by the key's first character, strcmp along each chain, malloc per new counter. C++: std::unordered_map<string,int> over a vector<string> with a custom hash returning s[0], cnt[*it] += 1. Lua: a plain table, `if map[text[i]] then map[text[i]] = map[text[i]] + 1`.
claimed_speedup: Original 2012 'benchmark' transcript (one `time` run each, real time): C 0.234 s, C++ 0.321 s, Node 0.317 s, LuaJIT 0.161 s, so LuaJIT 1.45x faster than C and 1.99x faster than C++ (derived from page data). Author's 2020-05-26 rerun comment (no versions or hardware): C 0.173 s, C++ 0.36 s, Node 0.5 s, LuaJIT 0.08 s (2.2x vs C, 4.5x vs C++, derived from page data); at 10x iterations LuaJIT 0.76 s, C 1.44 s, C++ 3.35 s (1.9x vs C, 4.4x vs C++, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 test.c; g++ -O3 -std=gnu++0x test.cpp; luajit test.lua with default options; no gcc, g++ or LuaJIT versions are given for the 2012 transcript or the 2020 rerun. The gcc 8.3.0, Node v15.12.0 and LuaJIT 2.0.5 named in mbossX's 2021 comment belong to that commenter's own separate 100M-iteration array-based programs (C 0.001 s, LuaJIT 1.774 s), not to the author's numbers.
stars_or_usage: 72 gist stars, 6 forks (2026-10-11); widely cited in LuaJIT vs C discussions
tradeoffs: Toy workload with a tiny hard-coded dictionary and pre-split words.
caveats: The author's a-warning.md (added 2015-08-18) says the benchmark 'has been misleading for a while': hard-coded text, small dictionary, pre-split words, no allocation cost. The author's own 2013 comment in test.lua says 'luajit probably optimizes away all dictionary lookups', which he did not verify. The C and C++ baselines use a first-character hash, so words sharing an initial letter collide and pay full string compares, while Lua strings are interned with a cached hash and compared by pointer; the author notes the default std::hash made C++ 2x slower. Timings are single `time` runs including process startup, with no CPU model and no compiler or LuaJIT versions. Comments show the C++ side can be beaten back: jh3141's fork (2014-12-06, g++ and clang++ -O3) reached 90 ms vs LuaJIT 95 ms and 71 ms with clang++, but it replaced the hash table with a vector of pairs plus a cached next-item pointer and interned pointers, a benchmark-specific structure that does not settle the hash-table comparison either; later array-based C versions (Zack24 2017, mbossX 2021) do no hashing. Source files last changed 2012-07-14 (test.c) and 2013-10-16 (test.lua comment only). No license.

name: Node.js (V8 Irregexp JIT) regex-dna in kostya/jit-benchmarks
baseline: C regex-dna (regexdna/test.c, Mike Pall's 2009-era Benchmarks Game program) using libpcre (PCRE1) with pcre_study(re, 0, ...), so PCRE's JIT is not enabled and every match runs in PCRE's interpreter; gcc 12.2.0 -O3 -march=native -fomit-frame-pointer -funroll-loops, linked with -lpcre
workload: Benchmarks Game regex-dna on a fasta file generated by regexdna/helper.c with n=3,500,000 (ONE 7M, TWO 10.5M and THREE 17.5M bases): nine case-insensitive variant-count regexes and eleven IUB-code substitutions after stripping headers and newlines; single thread, one process run, timed externally from the 'started' message (after input reading and line stripping) to process exit.
claimed_speedup: regexdna: Node 1.06s vs C 5.6s (about 5.3x, derived from page data), one measured run per row (Runs 1); memory 622.4 MB vs 86.7 MB. PHP (PCRE2 via preg_*) takes 1.39s (JIT) and 1.40s on the same nine caseless counts and eleven substitutions.
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc -O3 -march=native -fomit-frame-pointer -funroll-loops -Wno-unused-result -Wno-implicit-function-declaration ... -lpcre (tools/languages.rb c build_cmd plus tools/benchmarks.rb build_flags for regexdna); gcc 12.2.0 per README Versions; libpcre version not stated. Node.js 19.7.0 run as node test.js with default flags.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, 80 GB DDR4-3200, Docker on Ubuntu 22.10
tradeoffs: Node uses 622 MB vs 86.7 MB for the C program.
caveats: Crippled baseline: the C program calls pcre_study with flags 0, so libpcre runs its interpreter, while V8's Irregexp compiles each regex to native code; the comparison measures regex-engine mode (interpreted PCRE1 vs compiled Irregexp), not JavaScript against C. The PHP rows, which drive PCRE2 through preg_* with the same nine caseless counts and eleven substitutions (PHP's pcre.jit setting defaults to on), take 1.39s and 1.40s, 4x faster than the C row, so a C build with PCRE or PCRE2 JIT would likely land near Node. The Crystal row (0.34s) is not the same work: its test.cr does all eleven substitutions in one gsub pass with an alternation and a hash, uses case-sensitive variant regexes and maps S to (c|t), so it is no evidence for what JIT-enabled C would reach. The C program dates from before PCRE gained a JIT (PCRE 8.20, 2011). Single measured run per row (Runs 1). Numbers are from round 1 (2023-02-28) with node 19.7.0 and were not rerun; the only 2026 commit adds a README link. The README states no mechanism. The win belongs to V8's Irregexp engine (C++), not the JavaScript language.

name: Node.js (V8) fannkuch-redux in kostya/jit-benchmarks
baseline: C fannkuch-redux (fannkuchredux/test.c, the Benchmarks Game Java-derived program with variable-length arrays), gcc 12.2.0 -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops
workload: Benchmarks Game fannkuch-redux at n=10 (tools/benchmarks.rb args [10, TEST_COUNT], TEST_COUNT 5): one process runs the kernel 5 times and each run prints its own in-language time (C clock(), JS Date); Best T is the minimum of those in-process times, so start-up is excluded and JIT warm-up is largely excluded. Single thread.
claimed_speedup: fannkuchredux (README round 1, 2023-02-28): Node 0.15 s vs C 0.21 s best run (about 1.4x, derived from page data); GraalVM_JVM 0.18 s and GraalVM 0.19 s also below C; Lua JIT 0.27 s slower. Same table: Cython 0.13 s (Cython-generated C built with the same gcc flags, Pall-style flip loop) beats Node, and Crystal 0.19 s (same algorithm as the C program) roughly ties C.
compiler_and_flags: C/C++: gcc and g++ 12.2.0 with -O3 -march=native -fomit-frame-pointer -funroll-loops (C++ uses -std=c++11), from tools/languages.rb; luajit 2.1.0-beta3; nodejs 19.7.0

caveats: Not the same algorithm: test.js is Isaac Gouy's transliteration of Mike Pall's Lua program (caches the first element, writes q[q0]=q0, skips the swap loop when q0 < 3, sign-swap permutation step), while test.c is the Oleg Mazurov Java-derived program (reverses the full prefix including element 0 on every flip, VLA arrays). The suite's own Cython program, a Pall-style variant compiled by gcc with the same -O3 flags, runs in 0.13 s and beats Node's 0.15 s, so the Node win over C is algorithmic, not a JIT effect; README's 'one algorithm' promise does not hold for this benchmark. Timing is in-language (C clock() CPU time, JS Date wall time), best of 5 runs inside one process at n=10, so the earlier note that start-up is included was wrong. Numbers date from 2023-02-28 (gcc 12.2.0, nodejs 19.7.0); the only commit since 2023-03-30 is a README link (2026-01-27). name: OrdinaryDiffEq.jl (DifferentialEquations.jl) ODE solvers vs Sundials, ODEPACK and Hairer codes
baseline: Sundials CVODE_Adams and ARKODE (C), ODEPACK lsoda (Fortran) and Hairer dopri5/dop853/odex (Fortran), called through Julia wrappers
workload: Work-precision diagrams (wall time versus error at tolerances 1e-6 to 1e-13) for non-stiff ODEs: Lotka-Volterra, Pleiades and Three-Body.
claimed_speedup: SciMLBenchmarks README summary (no numbers): non-stiff 'OrdinaryDiffEq.jl's methods are the most efficient by a good amount', the Vern methods do best, ARKODE and Hairer dopri5/dop853 are 'far less efficient than the Vern methods', CVODE_Adams and lsoda 'tend to not do very well'; stiff: ARKODE is inconsistent and KenCarp4 is 'much more efficient in most cases'. Rigid Body work-precision plot (RigidBody_wpd_5_1, 3 equations, AMD EPYC 7502): Vern7/Vern8 take about 2e-5 to 1e-4 s while CVODE_Adams and ARKODE (explicit, order 6) take about 1e-4 to 1e-3 s over the same error range, roughly 5-10x at matched error (read off the plot, derived from page data). On the stiff Pollution page (20 equations) FBDF is only modestly ahead of CVODE_BDF in the high-tolerance plot, and the page's own conclusion reads 'Sundials CVODE_BDF the best here'.
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.11.9 (LLVM 16.0.6, znver2) for OrdinaryDiffEq; Sundials C library via Sundials.jl v6.7.1 and Sundials_jll v7.5.0+0 (BinaryBuilder build, compiler and flags not stated); ODEInterface_jll v0.0.2 and LSODA_jll v0.1.2 for the secondary baselines
hardware: AMD EPYC 7502 32-Core (128 threads), Linux; Julia 1.11.9, LLVM 16.0.6 (znver2), per the RigidBody and Pollution page appendices
tradeoffs: Julia JIT start-up and package precompilation; wins depend on the Verner high-order Runge-Kutta methods and algorithm-specific interpolation that the C and Fortran codes do not provide.
caveats: First-party suite run by the SciML project on its own solvers. Algorithm versus algorithm: Vern7/8/9 and Tsit5 against Dormand-Prince, Adams and ARKODE methods, so the win is not the language's (same_algorithm false). In this harness the Sundials C solvers are driven through Sundials.jl wrappers with a Julia right-hand side called back across the C boundary on every function evaluation, and each timed solve includes wrapper setup; on 3-equation problems solved in 20 microseconds to 1 ms this fixed overhead weighs heavily, and the Julia methods also get a StaticArrays out-of-place variant (prob_choice 2) that the C library cannot use. Numbers exist only as plots; the RigidBody page notes that some of the gap depends on each library's error norm. The win is not universal: on the stiff Pollution problem the page's conclusion names Sundials CVODE_BDF the best, and FBDF is only modestly ahead in its high-tolerance plot. Fortran baselines (dopri5, dop853, radau, ODEInterface) are out of scope for a C/C++ baseline.
found_via: Checked SciML/SciMLBenchmarksOutput markdown (NonStiffODE) after the Julia-vs-C++ WebSearch returned only forum threads.
why_faster: Pages credit the Verner methods and algorithm-specific interpolants; Julia specialization of the user's ODE function (FullSpecialize, StaticArrays) is implied by the setup but not argued as the cause.

verification.notes: Keep at C as an algorithm win, not a language win (same_algorithm false, language_level_claim false); benchmark_url moved to the RigidBody output page, which has the plots and the hardware appendix. Shortcomings: first-party, numbers only in plots, C solvers driven through Julia callbacks with wrapper setup inside the timing, Sundials_jll build flags unstated, and the Pollution page names CVODE_BDF the best.
