name: regex (Rust regex crate)
baseline: PCRE2 (interpreter and JIT) and RE2 (C/C++ regex engines); Hyperscan also measured
workload: rebar curated barometer: about 38 regex search benchmarks (literals, alternations, dates, Unicode classes, bounded repeats, dictionaries, ReDoS-style patterns, noseyparker rules) across many engines; corroborated by the LangArena Etc::LogParser task (13 log-grep patterns over generated web-server log lines).
claimed_speedup: rebar README summary of search-time benchmarks (geometric mean of per-benchmark speed ratios to the best engine, lower is better): hyperscan 2.37 (28 benchmarks), rust/regex 1.12.2 3.08 (38), pcre2/jit 10.47 6.00 (34), re2 10.39 (31), pcre2 interpreter 114.75 (33). The compile-time summary goes the other way: pcre2 1.41, pcre2/jit 6.20, rust/regex 11.85, re2 12.28. Intersection derived from the repo's recorded CSVs record/curated/2025-12-19/*.csv (median search times; derived from page data, re-computed by the verifier): vs PCRE2 JIT rust/regex is faster in 21 of 34 benchmarks, geometric-mean time ratio 2.13x; vs RE2 faster in 27 of 31, 4.3x; vs the PCRE2 interpreter faster in 32 of 33, 44x; vs Hyperscan faster in only 12 of 28 (Hyperscan about 1.45x faster overall). LangArena results 2026-10-05, Etc::LogParser (13 patterns, count all matches): Rust 0.302 s vs C with PCRE2 JIT 0.485 s (clang -O2), 0.488 s (gcc -O2) and 0.486 s (gcc -O3 -march=native 'Fast' build), about 1.6x; vs the C++ version, which uses RE2, 0.993-0.998 s (about 3.3x). In the same file, Template::Regex ({{(.*?)}} replacement): Rust 3.699 s vs C with PCRE2 JIT 1.155-1.173 s, so PCRE2 JIT is about 3.2x faster there; vs C++ RE2 4.84-4.90 s, Rust is about 1.3x faster.
compiler_and_flags: rebar: engine versions only (rust/regex 1.12.2, pcre2 10.47, re2 2025-11-05). PCRE2 (with SUPPORT_JIT) and RE2 are compiled from vendored source by the cc crate inside each engine's Cargo release profile (lto = fat, codegen-units = 1, default opt-level 3, so -O3 by the cc crate's default). This is derived from engines/pcre2/build.rs, engines/re2/build.rs and their Cargo.toml files; no compiler version is stated. LangArena: rustc 1.99.0, 'cargo build --release' with regex 1.12. C: clang 22.1.8 and gcc 16.0.1, prod flags -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer, Fast flags -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -funroll-loops with -flto=thin, linked against the system libpcre2-8. C++ is linked against the system libre2. The system PCRE2 and RE2 versions and build flags are not recorded in the results file.
hardware: rebar does not state the machine. LangArena results file: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X 8-Core Processor, 78 GB, x86_64 Linux.
why_faster: rebar analysis: finite-automata engines (lazy DFA, one-pass DFA) with SIMD literal prefilters (memchr, Teddy) avoid backtracking and give DFA-speed matching on most patterns; PCRE2 JIT stays faster where JIT-compiled backtracking is cheap (small anchored patterns, capture-heavy cases).
stars_or_usage: 4.0k stars; the regex engine behind ripgrep and much of the Rust ecosystem
tradeoffs: No backreferences or look-around (linear-time guarantee in exchange). Pattern compilation is slower than PCRE2 and RE2. Unicode tables add binary size. Rust API; C++ needs the rure C binding or FFI.
caveats: rebar's summary geometric means cover different benchmark subsets per engine (28 to 38), so only the intersection numbers compare like for like; the verifier re-computed them from the repo's recorded CSVs and they match. rebar is written by the regex crate's author, and its README says the analysis is biased towards that crate (BIAS.md). rebar states no CPU or compiler version. Hyperscan beats regex overall, and PCRE2 JIT wins 13 of the 34 shared benchmarks. LangArena is independent, with public code, compilers, flags and CPU. Its C LogParser time is the same at -O2 and at -O3 -march=native (0.486 s), so the opt level does not explain the gap. The PCRE2 and RE2 it measures are system libraries whose versions and build flags are not recorded. The C++ LangArena rows use RE2, not PCRE2. LangArena's Template::Regex task shows a 3.2x loss to PCRE2 JIT. The win is a library and engine-design effect (lazy DFA plus SIMD literal prefilters), not a language effect.
found_via: WebSearch 'Rust crate "faster than glibc" string search OR strstr OR strtod OR memmem benchmark SIMD' surfaced memchr and rebar; then opened rebar README (raw.githubusercontent.com) and its record/curated/2025-12-19 CSVs, and kostya/LangArena results/2026-10-05-kostya-ms7c37.js (https://github.com/kostya/LangArena/blob/master/results/2026-10-05-kostya-ms7c37.js).

verification.tier_reason: Tier A rests on the independent LangArena suite: its benchmark code is public (c/src/log_parser.c with pcre2_jit_match, rust/src/benchmarks/log_parser.rs with regex::Regex::find_iter, the same 13 patterns and count-all-matches work). Its results file results/2026-10-05-kostya-ms7c37.js states the CPU (AMD Ryzen 7 3800X), clang 22.1.8, gcc 16.0.1 and rustc 1.99.0, and the C flags are in c/Makefile. rebar alone would be tier C: it is written by the regex crate's author, it lists engine versions but no CPU or compiler version, and its flags are only derivable from Cargo profiles.
verification.notes: Every number checked: the rebar README summary tables, the intersection ratios re-computed from the 2025-12-19 CSVs (21/34 at 2.13x vs PCRE2 JIT, 27/31 at 4.3x vs RE2, 32/33 at 44x vs the PCRE2 interpreter, 12/28 at 0.69x vs Hyperscan) and the LangArena runtimes all match. Shortcomings: rebar is first-party and states no CPU; regex loses to Hyperscan overall, loses to PCRE2 JIT on about a third of rebar's benchmarks and on LangArena Template::Regex (3.2x); LangArena's baselines are system-packaged PCRE2 and RE2 with unrecorded versions and flags. Metadata confirmed: MIT OR Apache-2.0, 4.0k stars, last commit 2026-08-10. Not a duplicate: ripgrep (wave 11) is listed separately and uses this crate.

name: A*PA2 (astar-pairwise-aligner)
baseline: Edlib (C++) and BiWFA / WFA2-lib (C) exact global aligners
workload: Exact global pairwise alignment (edit distance) of long DNA sequences, e.g. ONT reads of a human genome with 6% to 11% divergence, plus synthetic sequences.
claimed_speedup: Repo README: 'It achieves up to 20x speedup over other exact aligners and is competitive with approximate aligners' (the WABI paper title says 'up to 19x faster'). pa-bench evals/astarpa2/evals.ipynb saved output: mean speedup of A*PA2-simple over Edlib 7.48 on the scaling-n synthetic set and 8.26 on the scaling-e set (notebook output). Its runtime table, with a 'best A*PA2 vs best of Edlib/BiWFA' speedup row, has no saved output. Paper abstract, seen only in a search snippet (WABI 2024, LIPIcs 312; paper page blocked): 19x faster than BiWFA and Edlib on >500 kbp ONT reads with 6% divergence; 5.6x on 11 kbp reads with 11% divergence; 0.81x (slower) on 800 bp reads with 11% divergence.
compiler_and_flags: pa-bench release profile: lto = true, codegen-units = 1 (pa-bench Cargo.toml); A*PA2 is pulled in as a git dependency, and its repo pins a nightly toolchain (rust-toolchain.toml). The aligner repo's .cargo/config.toml sets -C target-cpu=native, but pa-bench does not state which RUSTFLAGS the paper runs used. Edlib is built by edlib-rs through the cmake crate; its build.rs passes '-D CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release' as a C flag, so the build type comes from the cmake crate's profile mapping (derived). The rust-wfa2 build for BiWFA was not checked.
hardware: CPU model not stated in pa-bench; evals/astarpa2/justfile pins the CPU at 3.6 GHz with cpupower (performance governor), and pa-bench pins each job to one core.
why_faster: Per the paper snippet: like Edlib it uses Ukkonen band doubling with Myers bit-packing, adding large blocks, SIMD, a new profile and the A* heuristics from A*PA (a different algorithm, not a language effect).
tradeoffs: Gains only on long, low-divergence inputs; slower than Edlib on short, highly divergent reads. Latest commit message mentions 'latest nightly', so a nightly Rust toolchain may be needed (not confirmed). MPL-2.0 is file-level copyleft. Evaluation harness lives in a separate pa-bench repo.
caveats: The paper's 19x, 5.6x and 0.81x figures are snippet only, because the LIPIcs and bioRxiv pages are blocked here. What could be opened is the author's own README claim and the pa-bench notebook. The full results live in a release results.zip that was not opened. No CPU model is stated in the repos. The speedup comes from a different algorithm: band doubling with Myers bit-packing plus blocks, SIMD, a new profile and the A* heuristics. It is not a Rust-vs-C++ language effect, and A*PA2 is slower than Edlib and BiWFA on short (800 bp) high-divergence reads. Pairwise alignment is on the edge of the string-and-text category.
found_via: WebSearch 'A*PA2 exact global sequence alignment Rust faster than Edlib WFA github astarpa2'; opened the repo page and commits feed.

name: needletail (Rust FASTA/FASTQ parser)
baseline: kseq.h from klib (C FASTA/FASTQ parser)
workload: Parsing a 4-line FASTQ file of 5,682,010 records and counting records, sequence length and quality length; plain and gzip-compressed input.
claimed_speedup: lh3/biofast README and fqcnt/README.md, fqcnt table (CPU seconds, hyperfine average): needletail plain 0.8 s vs C kseq.h 1.4 s (1.75x, derived from page data); gzip input 9.3 s vs 9.7 s (about equal, since decompression dominates). For reference, rust-bio in the same table is 2.4 s plain and 10.0 s gzip.
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc-4.8.5 with -g -Wall -O2 (fqcnt/Makefile), not -O3. Rust: 'cargo install' (release profile, default opt-level 3) with needletail = "0.4" (biofast Cargo.toml); rustc version not stated.
hardware: CentOS 7 server with two EPYC 7301 CPUs and 1 TB memory
tradeoffs: Rust API (no C++ binding in repo). Parses FASTA and 4-line FASTQ only, while the baseline kseq.h also handles multi-line records, which the biofast table marks in its comments column.
caveats: This is an independent benchmark by the author of kseq.h, but it dates from 2020 and measured needletail 0.4 (the current README shows 0.6.0), so the numbers are stale. The C baseline is gcc-4.8.5 at -O2, not -O3. Plain-file C input still goes through zlib's gzread, and needletail handles only 4-line FASTQ against kseq.h's multi-line parser, which favours needletail. gzip input shows no gain (9.3 s vs 9.7 s). Needletail's own README claims only to aim to be 'as fast as the readfq C library' and has no benchmark section. The Crystal, Nim and Julia ports of kseq.h do not beat C in the same table.
found_via: Searched for cross-language text-parsing shootouts; opened lh3/biofast README (fqcnt table) and needletail repo page and commits feed.

name: Sassy (SIMD approximate string matching)
baseline: Edlib (C++ Myers bit-vector aligner); parasail (C) and SWOffinder also compared in the paper
workload: Searching short DNA/ASCII patterns (up to about 1000 characters) in long texts allowing k edit errors, synthetic data and a human genome search.
claimed_speedup: Paper abstract (Bioinformatics, May 2026; repo copy in doc/abstract.md): Sassy1 is 4-15x faster than Edlib for patterns up to 1000 bp and reaches a text throughput up to 2 Gbp/s; for CRISPR off-target detection of 61 guides in a human genome it is 100x faster than SWOffinder and only slightly slower than the index-based CHOPOFF. 'Over 100x faster than parasail' appears in the published abstract only as quoted by a WebSearch snippet (snippet only; not in the repo copy). Sassy2 (bioRxiv, March 2026) is an additional 10-50x faster than Sassy1 for short (<200 bp) texts and 2.5-4.5x for long (>8 kbp) texts; README: Sassy2 2x faster with AVX-512 and pre-encoded patterns 10-20x faster for short texts (internal comparisons).
compiler_and_flags: Sassy: Rust >= 1.91, release profile opt-level 3 (debug info on; dist profile adds LTO and one codegen unit) with .cargo/config.toml target-cpu=native; the Edlib eval is built with 'cargo build --release -p evals'. Edlib (C++) is called through edlib-rs, whose build.rs uses the cmake crate; the cmake crate derives CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE from the Cargo profile, and with sassy's release profile (debug = true) that is RelWithDebInfo (CMake default -O2 -g), with no -march=native; edlib-rs's .cflag("-D CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release") only adds a C preprocessor define and Edlib's CMakeLists sets no build type. Parasail built from its CMake (flags unstated, striped SSE4.1/AVX2 kernels tried); Ish built with ISH_SIMD_TARGET=sse.
why_faster: Bit-packing with SIMD (AVX2/NEON) where the bit-vectors run along the text direction ('tiling in the text direction'), with the text split into 4 parts searched in parallel; complexity O(k ceil(n/W)) with W=256.
stars_or_usage: 169 stars, 18 forks; crates.io 6101 downloads (2287 recent, v0.2.6); also on bioconda and PyPI (sassy-rs); third-party DuckDB/R bindings (ducksassy)
tradeoffs: Needs AVX2 or NEON; supports ASCII, DNA and IUPAC alphabets; best for patterns up to about 1000; C bindings, Python bindings and a CLI exist.
caveats: Edlib numbers come from the peer-reviewed paper's abstract (repo copy doc/abstract.md); the full paper, its hardware and the eval CSVs were not opened (bioRxiv, doi.org and the KIT library PDF host were unreachable). The win is algorithmic, not a language effect: Sassy tiles bit-vectors along the text with 256-bit AVX2 lanes over 4 text chunks, while Edlib runs scalar 64-bit Myers/Hyyro bit-vectors. In the public evals harness Edlib is probably compiled at RelWithDebInfo (-O2 -g, generic x86-64) while Sassy gets opt-level 3 plus target-cpu=native, so optimisation levels are not matched (not a crippled -O0 build). The parasail >100x figure is snippet only. Requires AVX2 or NEON at compile time (scalar feature is slower).
found_via: WebSearch 'Sassy SIMD approximate string matching DNA Rust faster than Edlib speedup'; opened README, evals/README.md and repo page.

verification.tier_reason: Peer-reviewed Bioinformatics article (May 2026, doi 10.1093/bioinformatics/btag244) whose abstract, checked into the repo as doc/abstract.md, reports Sassy1 4-15x faster than Edlib for patterns up to 1000 bp; the harness (evals/, run_tool_bench.py, edlib-rs and parasail-rs dependencies) is public, but no CPU model or Edlib build flags are stated in the repo and the paper itself was unreachable, so not A.
verification.notes: Abstract in repo confirms the 4-15x vs Edlib and 100x vs SWOffinder claims; parasail >100x is snippet only. Shortcomings to record: algorithmic win (text-direction SIMD tiling vs scalar Myers), Edlib likely built -O2 -g without native tuning in the evals harness via edlib-rs/cmake crate while Sassy uses target-cpu=native, hardware unstated in repo.

name: eBay TSV Utilities (D)
baseline: GNU awk 4.2.1, mawk 1.3.3, GNU cut 8.25 and GNU Datamash 1.3 (all C)
workload: Six command-line tasks on multi-GB delimited text: numeric row filter and regex row filter (4.8 GB / 2.7 GB), column selection (wide and narrow lines), file join, summary statistics, CSV-to-TSV; also compared with xsv (Rust) and csvtk (Go).
claimed_speedup: 2018 first-party study, Linux (16-CPU Intel Haswell 2095 MHz cloud machine), seconds, 10th percentile of 35 runs: numeric row filter tsv-filter 5.48 vs mawk 11.31 vs GNU awk 42.80 (about 2.1x and 7.8x, derived from page data); column selection (4.8 GB) tsv-select 4.79 vs mawk 9.51 vs GNU cut 14.46 (about 3.0x vs cut, derived); summary statistics tsv-summarize 15.78 vs GNU Datamash 48.51 (about 3.1x, derived); regex row filter tsv-filter 8.80 vs mawk 17.74 vs GNU awk 29.02, but xsv (Rust) 7.97 is faster; narrow-line column selection (86M short lines) GNU cut 5.60 beats tsv-select 8.26. MacOS (Mac mini, 2-core 3 GHz i7): numeric filter 3.35 vs mawk 15.06 vs GNU awk 24.25; narrow column selection tsv-select 10.18 vs GNU cut 10.65. Independent hck README (AMD Ryzen 9 3950X, hyperfine, comma-delimited 7M-line HEPMASS CSV): tsv-select v2.2.0 1.702 s vs GNU cut 8.30 7.541 s (about 4.4x, derived from page data; about 4.0x on min times 1.687 vs 6.827) and vs awk 4.993 s (about 2.9x, derived); hck itself is faster at 1.198 s.
compiler_and_flags: 2018 study: tsv-utils v1.1.19 prebuilt release binaries (LDC; the page credits LTO and PGO for the 2018 gains); GNU awk 4.2.1, mawk 1.3.3/1.3.4, GNU cut 8.25/8.29 and GNU Datamash 1.3 from standard package managers (build flags not stated). hck run: tsv-utils v2.2.0 compiled locally with ldc2 'with optimizations'; GNU cut 8.30 and mawk 1.3.4 from Ubuntu 20 (flags not stated).
hardware: 2018 study, Linux: 16 CPU Intel Haswell 2095 MHz, 32 GB RAM, Ubuntu 16.04 cloud machine; MacOS: Mac mini, 3 GHz Intel i7 (2 cores), 16 GB, MacOS 10.13.3. hck run: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X 16-core, 64 GB DDR4, NVMe, Ubuntu 20.
why_faster: Author's stated reasons: straightforward D with avoidance of GC allocation, LDC link-time and profile-guided optimisation (2018 gain), TSV-only data model (no CSV escape handling, which the docs call computationally more expensive); the tools are single-threaded, so none of the gain is from parallelism.
stars_or_usage: 1.5k stars, 84 forks; prebuilt Linux and macOS binaries
tradeoffs: TSV-only (no CSV escapes except csv2tsv); a toolkit of single-purpose tools rather than awk-like scripting; D toolchain needed to build.
caveats: The 2018 study is first-party and 8 years old; the author frames it as a gauge of D performance, not a like-for-like language comparison. The awk rows compare a specialised compiled filter against a general-purpose awk interpreter running a script per line, and Datamash was fed through 'cat |', so same_algorithm is false; the closest like-for-like baseline is GNU cut, which wins the Linux narrow-line test (5.60 vs 8.26 s). Unmatched optimisation: the D tools are LDC builds with LTO and PGO while the C tools are distro package binaries (typically -O2, not crippled). xsv (Rust) wins regex filtering. tsv-utils is single-threaded, so no gain is from parallelism. The independent hck numbers (a competitor's README that says it is not authoritative) cover only column selection; GNU cut's 7.541 s mean has a 1.250 s spread. Repo has no commits since 2021-06-13 (abandoned, not archived).
found_via: QUEUE.md cross-wave lead 'eBay/tsv-utils'; opened README, docs/Performance.md, docs/comparative-benchmarks-2018.md and the hck README benchmark table.

Shortcomings: specialised tool vs awk interpreters, LTO+PGO D builds vs distro C binaries, GNU cut wins narrow lines, xsv wins regex, abandoned since 2021.

name: fastgrep (Rust grep)
baseline: GNU grep 3.12 (C)
workload: Recursive searches over a generated corpus of 200 files x 5,000 lines of Rust-like source (sparse and dense matches, case-insensitive, regex, single 100k-line file) and a scaling test of 50 to 500 files.
claimed_speedup: README benchmark table (warm trigram index, LC_ALL=C): -rn 'fn main' 8.82 ms vs GNU grep 32.99 ms (3.74x); -rc 'use ' 8.55 ms vs 84.75 ms (9.91x); -rni error 37.49 ms vs 82.57 ms (2.20x); -rn 'impl\s+Drop' 45.24 vs 73.43 (1.62x); very sparse SubscriptionManager 5.41 vs 39.35 (7.28x); single file 3.70 vs 5.21 (1.41x); but -rl 'fn main' 7.50 ms vs GNU grep 7.12 ms (0.95x, GNU grep faster). Scaling: 1.48x at 50 files, 2.43x at 200, 3.08x at 500.
compiler_and_flags: fastgrep 0.1.9 at commit 5094623, Rust 1.99.0, repository release profile: opt-level = "s", LTO, codegen-units 1, panic = abort, stripped; Criterion 0.8.2, one subprocess per iteration with output captured in memory, warm filesystem cache, LC_ALL=C, default thread counts. GNU grep 3.12 is Homebrew's ggrep (build flags not stated).
hardware: Apple M2 Max (12 logical CPUs), 32 GB, macOS 27.0.1
why_faster: README: parallel by default across all CPU threads, lazy trigram index that skips non-matching files on repeat searches, SIMD-accelerated literal search.
stars_or_usage: 2 stars; crates.io 431 downloads (113 recent), current version 0.1.10
tradeoffs: Output order is non-deterministic (multi-threaded); deliberate deviations from GNU grep (binary files, long lines). Index cache stored under the OS cache directory and invalidated by mtime and size. Not every GNU grep flag implemented.
caveats: Very new (crate first published 2026-03-04), first-party numbers on a small synthetic corpus (about 1M lines; runs of 4-85 ms that include process start-up). The win is mostly 12-thread parallelism against single-threaded GNU grep: the --no-index mode is faster than the default warm-index mode in 4 of the 5 indexed rows (e.g. 7.31 vs 8.82 ms on 'fn main', 7.64 vs 8.55 ms on 'use '), and the index helps only on the very sparse query (5.41 vs 6.30 ms); every file contains 'fn main', 'use ' and 'impl Drop', so the index cannot skip files for them. No per-thread or single-threaded comparison is published, so no faster per-byte scan is shown (literal and regex search come from the memchr and regex crates). GNU grep wins -rl (7.12 vs 7.50 ms). fastgrep is built at opt-level s (size), not a speed-tuned build, while GNU grep is a Homebrew bottle with unstated flags. Deliberate behaviour differences (100 MiB file-size limit, 15000-byte line truncation, unordered parallel output) change semantics versus GNU grep.

name: jumprope (Rust rope)
baseline: librope (C skip-list rope by the same author)
workload: Replaying real text-editing traces (automerge-paper, rustcode, sveltecomponent, seph-blog1) from crdt-benchmarks against a rope: insert/delete at arbitrary positions.
claimed_speedup: README table, single core of a Ryzen 5800X: automerge-paper librope (C) 16.28 ms vs Jumprope 6.66 ms; rustcode 3.93 vs 1.66 ms; sveltecomponent 1.59 vs 0.59 ms; seph-blog1 10.01 vs 3.81 ms (about 2.4x to 2.7x, derived from page data). README also says jumprope is about 3x faster than ropey (a Rust rope) on real editing operations, and its JumpRopeBuf wrapper (merges runs of edits before applying them) is claimed about 10x faster again.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the README. Workspace Cargo.toml release profile: lto = true, codegen-units = 1 (Rust side). rope_benches/build.rs compiles a vendored rope.c with cc::Build defaults (no explicit flags, no NDEBUG; cc follows Cargo's release opt-level), linked as a static library with no cross-language LTO, so every C call crosses an FFI boundary. Run with 'cargo run --release -- --bench' in rope_benches.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 5800X, single core
why_faster: README: jumprope is a skip list whose leaf nodes each contain a gap buffer, versus librope's plain skip list.
license: ISC (LICENSE.txt and README); Cargo.toml declares ISC OR Apache-2.0
tradeoffs: Fewer features than ropey (no line/column conversion). Meant for large documents; the README recommends std String for strings under about 100 bytes.
caveats: First-party numbers from the author, who also wrote the C baseline. The README table was last updated on 2021-10-05/06 (README commit history), before jumprope 1.0 (2022), so it does not reflect the current code. Benchmark code is public (rope_benches/src/main.rs, criterion 'realworld' group) but loads traces from a hard-coded /home/seph/src/diamond-types/benchmark_data path; compiler versions and C flags are unstated. Harness asymmetry: the C column ('C-JumpRope' in the code) is a vendored copy of librope's rope.c built by the cc crate without NDEBUG and driven through FFI with a CString allocation and copy per insert inside the timed loop, while Jumprope takes &str directly inside the same LTO-built Rust binary; this inflates the 2.4-2.7x gap by an unmeasured amount. The realworld check compares only the final char_len, not the content. Algorithms differ (gap-buffer leaves vs plain skip-list nodes), so the win is data-structure design rather than language. librope itself is already catalogued (wave 1, https://github.com/josephg/librope) from the same table; this record is its Rust successor, not a duplicate. The linked criterion report host (home.seph.codes) does not resolve (ENOTFOUND). No commits since 2023-05-20.

name: Vibrato (Rust MeCab reimplementation)
baseline: MeCab (C++ Japanese morphological analyzer), 2020-09-14 build
workload: Tokenize all 2,346 lines (158.8 characters on average) of 'I Am a Cat' (Aozora Bunko). Each tool reads the lines into memory, then times only the tokenization loop with a steady clock, single-threaded. run_all.sh runs 101 iterations, each a fresh process, and iteration 0 is a warm-up. MeCab uses mecab-ipadic 2.7.0 or unidic-cwj 3.1.1, and Vibrato uses its v0.5.0 precompiled dictionaries built from the same sources. The MeCab driver calls tagger->parse() with -Owakati, which builds a space-separated output string. The Vibrato driver calls worker.tokenize() and only counts tokens.
claimed_speedup: Wiki Speed-Comparison table: Vibrato 0.5.0 ipadic 42 ms vs MeCab ipadic 87 ms (about 2.1x, derived from page data); Vibrato unidic-cwj 75 ms vs MeCab unidic-cwj 179 ms (about 2.4x, derived from page data); the Vibrato raw-connector variant takes 1364 ms (7.6x slower than MeCab) and dual-connector 170 ms (about equal).
compiler_and_flags: From tokenizer-speed-bench compile_all.sh (tag vibrato-0.5.0-benchmark): MeCab (taku910/mecab submodule) is built with its own ./configure, whose configure.in sets CFLAGS/CXXFLAGS to '-O3 -Wall' under GCC. The MeCab driver is built with 'g++ -std=c++11 -O3 ./main.cc -lmecab'. The Vibrato 0.5.0 crate is built with RUSTFLAGS='-C target-feature=+avx2' cargo build --release (release profile, opt-level 3). No gcc or rustc version is stated, and MeCab gets no -march, so only the Rust side is built for AVX2.
hardware: Intel Core i9-12900K, 64 GB DDR5, Ubuntu 22.04
why_faster: README: reimplementation of the MeCab algorithm simplified and optimised; for dictionaries with a large connection matrix (unidic-cwj, 459 MiB) cache-efficient id mappings make it faster.
tradeoffs: Rust library, C++ needs FFI or the CLI. Uses its own compiled dictionary format (zstd compressed system.dic.zst), converted from MeCab dictionaries; MeCab-compatible output options exist.
caveats: First-party benchmark run by the authors' organisation (LegalForce / daac-tools): one corpus (one novel) on one machine. Compiler versions are not stated. The two sides do not do equal work. (1) MeCab's parse() with -Owakati formats an output string, while Vibrato only builds the lattice and counts tokens. (2) Vibrato runs with default settings, not the MeCab-compatible -S -M 24 options, so its tokens can differ from MeCab's (README 'MeCab-compatible options'), and outputs were not compared. (3) Only Vibrato is compiled with AVX2 (+avx2); MeCab uses generic x86-64 -O3. (4) MeCab mmaps its dictionary and 459 MiB unidic matrix, so the timed loop likely pays page faults that Vibrato, which reads the whole dictionary into memory before timing, does not. This is an inference from the harness, not a measurement. The raw-connector compact model (1364 ms) is 7.6x slower than MeCab, and the dual-connector model (170 ms) is roughly level with it. The speedup is largest with the large-matrix unidic dictionary. The numbers are for Vibrato 0.5.0 (early 2023) and have not been re-run for later releases.
found_via: Searched for Rust reimplementations with a C++ baseline (tokenizers); opened vibrato README and its Speed-Comparison wiki page.

verification.tier_reason: The wiki Speed-Comparison page (last edited 2023-03-01) has first-party times for Vibrato 0.5.0 and MeCab 2020-09-14 on an i9-12900K. The harness is public (legalforce-research/tokenizer-speed-bench, tag vibrato-0.5.0-benchmark: compile_all.sh, run_all.sh, bench/mecab-unidic-3_1_1-bench/main.cc, bench/vibrato-bench/src/main.rs) and its flags are visible, but neither the g++ nor the rustc version is stated anywhere. Under the project's precedent a missing compiler version keeps it out of A, and the authors' own run is not B, so it stays C.
verification.notes: Numbers match the wiki exactly: ipadic 42 vs 87 ms (2.07x) and unidic 75 vs 179 ms (2.39x), derived from page data. The baseline is MeCab built at -O3 by its own configure, so the C++ side is not crippled. The gain is a reimplementation with a different data layout (cache-efficient id mapping of the connection matrix) plus a lighter timed path, not a Rust codegen effect. Shortcomings to record: no compiler versions, AVX2 only on the Vibrato side, MeCab formats -Owakati output while Vibrato only counts tokens, outputs not checked equal (non-compatible default mode), and likely mmap page faults inside MeCab's timed loop (inference).

name: ipnsort and driftsort (Rust std slice::sort_unstable and slice::sort)
baseline: C++ standard library sorts: std::sort and std::stable_sort of libstdc++ and libc++ (benchmark variants cpp_std_gnu / cpp_std_libcxx in the repo)
workload: Sorting 10k u64 values with a hot cache across seven input patterns (ascending, descending, random, random_d20, random_p5, random_s95, random_z1) on Zen 3; unstable contestants include rust_ipnsort_unstable (research-repo commit 757478b) and the pre-2024 Rust std sorts vendored mid 2022; MSVC rows are listed but not in the Linux plots.
claimed_speedup: Plot values in writeup/sort_safety/assets/unstable-hot-u64-10k.png (10k u64, hot, Zen 3, time in us): rust_ipnsort_unstable vs libstdc++ std::sort / libc++ std::sort: ascending 2.07 vs 49.3 / 6.23 (23.8x / 3.0x), descending 3.16 vs 32.2 / 11.4 (10.2x / 3.6x), random 77.0 vs 297.6 / 265.1 (3.9x / 3.4x), random_d20 24.3 vs 136.5 / 97.6 (5.6x / 4.0x), random_p5 12.4 vs 57.2 / 16.7 (4.6x / 1.35x), random_s95 83.4 vs 182.2 / 84.2 (2.2x / 1.01x), random_z1 56.8 vs 222.9 / 200.2 (3.9x / 3.5x) (ratios derived from page data). The text's 'current Rust standard library unstable sort ... outperforms the C++ standard library counterparts' refers to the pre-2024 pdqsort-based rust_std_unstable (random 136.9 us). Stable plot: driftsort is not tested; the then-current rust_std_stable beats libstdc++ std::stable_sort on random (253.0 vs 318.6 us) but loses on random_d20 (250.5 vs 190.5) and random_p5 (156.8 vs 69.8) and loses to libc++ on random, random_d20 and random_z1.
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.75.0-nightly (2023-10-03) with --release and lto=thin; C/C++ built through build.rs with opt_level(3) and -std=c++20 (-march=native only for the AVX2/AVX-512 contestants); clang 16.0.6 and gcc 13.2.1. The libstdc++ and libc++ variants are separate cargo features (cpp_std_sys, cpp_std_libcxx).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X (Zen 3), Linux 6.5, CPU boost enabled
stars_or_usage: 545 stars; ipnsort and driftsort replaced the sorts in the Rust standard library (rust-lang/rust PR 124032)
tradeoffs: Generic over Ord with arbitrary user comparators; written with a lot of unsafe Rust for code-gen reasons but designed to avoid UB on non-strict-weak orderings and panics (the writeup's Ord and exception safety analysis). Needs Rust; stable sort needs auxiliary memory.
caveats: Bias disclaimer: the ipnsort author wrote the analysis. Only 10k u64 on one CPU with 2023 toolchains (rustc 1.75 nightly, gcc 13.2.1, clang 16.0.6); the bitsetsort-derived libc++ std::sort of LLVM 17 is 'so far untested'. Driftsort (today's slice::sort) does not appear in this benchmark or in any C++ comparison found (the driftsort and ipnsort introductions compare only against Rust sorts), so the stable half of the record has no evidence against C++; the Rust stable sort shown (rust_std_stable, vendored mid 2022) is slower than libstdc++ std::stable_sort on random_d20 and random_p5 and slower than libc++ on random, random_d20 and random_z1. The ipnsort tested is the research-repo version at 757478b, not necessarily the code merged into std by rust-lang/rust PR 124032 (merged 2024-06-20). name: fd
baseline: GNU find (findutils, C)
workload: Search the author's home folder (about 750,000 subdirectories and about 4 million files) for names ending in [0-9].jpg with a warm disk cache, timed with hyperfine. The commands were find ~ -iregex '.*[0-9]\.jpg$', find ~ -iname '*[0-9].jpg' and fd -u '[0-9]\.jpg$' ~ (fd-benchmarks warm-cache-simple-pattern.sh uses fd -HI, 5 warm-up runs, and diffs the outputs). Both tools returned the same 546 files.
claimed_speedup: fd -u '[0-9]\.jpg$' 854.8 ms vs find -iregex 19.922 s (README: approximately 23 times faster) and vs find -iname 11.226 s (about 13 times faster).
tradeoffs: Respects .gitignore and skips hidden files by default (the benchmark needs -u to match find's work); regex search by default instead of glob; parallel traversal uses all cores.
caveats: First-party benchmark on one unnamed machine against the author's own home directory. The README says 'one particular benchmark on one particular machine'. fd, find and compiler versions are not stated, and nor is GNU find's build (distribution packages are usually -O2). fd walks directories in parallel with one thread per core by default, while GNU find is single-threaded. The task is dominated by pattern matching: find -iregex uses gnulib regex on the full path, and -iname uses case-folding fnmatch. Without a pattern the gap disappears. In sharkdp/fd issue #304 (2018, fd 7.0-7.1, Linux source tree, warm cache, no hardware stated), multi-threaded fd -HI -t f only reached parity with 'find . -type f' (69.1 ms vs 68.9 ms after commit 50a2bab), and fd -j1 was 1.49x slower than find. In the reporter's home-directory runs find was 2.15x (warm) and 1.85x (cold) faster than fd 7.0.0. So the README's 13-23x is a parallelism plus regex-engine win on a filtering query, not a codegen win, and single-threaded fd is slower than find on plain traversal. The README credits the regex and ignore crates (shared with ripgrep).

V/gcc, which emits C and compiles it with gcc, is faster than the C row, which points to data-layout and codegen variance rather than a language advantage. name: skani
baseline: FastANI 1.33 (C++) and Mash 2.3 (C++), bioconda builds pinned in skani-test/env.yml
workload: Average nucleotide identity computation between prokaryotic genomes and against a database of more than 65,000 genomes.
claimed_speedup: README: sketching about 3x faster than Mash, querying about 25x faster than FastANI but slower than Mash; v0.4.0 (October 2026) claims about 2x faster than v0.3. Paper abstract (snippet only): >20x faster than FastANI on fragmented, incomplete MAGs. Paper benchmark repo skani-test, /bin/time outputs at 50 threads (derived from page data): all-vs-all on 195 MAGs, skani triangle 3.30 s vs FastANI 2:58.96 (54x wall; 154.75 s vs 7142.43 s user, 46x); E. coli D3 database query, skani search 4.17 s (plus 3.55 s sketching) vs FastANI 2:44.50 (39x query-only, 21x including sketching); RefSeq all-vs-all, skani sketch 3.10 s plus triangle 11.38 s vs FastANI 3:02:24 (about 750x). Against Mash: skani sketching 3.55 s vs 18.19 s on D3 and 3.10 s vs 14.79 s on RefSeq (about 5x), but Mash dist on D3 takes 0.26 s vs skani search 4.17 s (skani 16x slower), and Mash triangle on the 195 MAGs takes 0.55 s vs 3.30 s.
compiler_and_flags: skani: prebuilt binary checked into skani-test (cargo release build; flags not stated). FastANI 1.33 (fastani=1.33=h0fdf51a_1) and Mash 2.3 (mash=2.3=ha9a2dd8_3) from bioconda, build flags those of the bioconda recipes.
hardware: CPU model not stated; 50 threads (/bin/time reports 3500-4950% CPU)
stars_or_usage: 265 stars, 15 forks; Nature Methods 2023 paper (doi 10.1038/s41592-023-02018-3); bioconda package; pyskani Python bindings by a third party
tradeoffs: Approximate ANI without base-level alignment; accuracy is 'almost as accurate' as BLAST-based methods per README.
caveats: The speedup is algorithmic, not a language effect: skani does approximate mapping with sparse chaining of k-mer seeds and no base-level alignment, while FastANI uses Mashmap-style mapping of 3 kb fragments, so same_algorithm is false and the Rust-vs-C++ question is not answered. skani is slower than Mash at querying (16x on D3, 6x on the 195-MAG triangle) and only beats it at sketching. The timings come from the paper-era binary in skani-test, not the current v0.4.0. No CPU model is given, and the FastANI and Mash builds are bioconda defaults. The RefSeq row compares outputs filtered differently (skani -E edge list vs FastANI full output), so the ~750x figure is indicative only. The skani README says a C compiler is needed to build (C dependency). The README's 25x figure has no raw numbers on the README page itself. The wave-14 category is a poor fit, since the win comes from the method, not the language.
found_via: Rust bioinformatics tools with C++ incumbents; skani README
why_faster: README: approximate mapping with sparse chaining of seed matches instead of base-level alignment.

verification.tier_reason: Upgraded from C. The peer-reviewed Nature Methods 2023 paper (abstract seen via snippet: >20x faster than FastANI on fragmented MAGs) has a public benchmark repo, bluenote-1577/skani-test, whose time_results.sh and time_2328_results.sh run skani, FastANI 1.33 and Mash 2.3 (bioconda pins in env.yml) under /bin/time -v, with the outputs checked into times/. It is not A because no CPU model or compiler flags are given.
verification.notes: Upgraded to B with verdict confirm: the peer-reviewed paper's public benchmark repo (skani-test) holds scripts and /bin/time outputs showing skani 21x-54x faster than FastANI 1.33 at 50 threads, but no CPU model. Shortcomings: an algorithmic win, not a language one (different method from FastANI); slower than Mash for querying; paper-era binary; CPU model absent. baseline_in_list corrected to false, since FastANI and Mash are not in the verified lists.

name: Supersnappy
baseline: Google Snappy (C++), called through its C API (snappy_compress, snappy_uncompress, snappy_validate_compressed_buffer) from a prebuilt libsnappy.dll loaded by the nimsnappy wrapper (version and build flags unknown; the wrapper says it tracks 1.1.3). Also Andi Kleen's snappy-c (C), compiled from source into the benchmark through the nimsnappyc wrapper's {.compile.} pragma. The pure-Nim status-im/nim-snappy is the fourth column.
workload: Snappy benchmark corpus (alice29.txt, asyoulik.txt, fireworks.jpg, geo.protodata, html, html_x_4, kppkn.gtb, lcet10.txt, paper-100k.pdf, plrabn12.txt, urls.10K). tests/bench.nim times one compress plus one uncompress of the whole file per benchy timeIt sample, with 1000 samples (x1000). The README header's '100 compress-uncompress cycles' does not match the current code.
claimed_speedup: README: 'performs significantly better in all cases than alternatives'. Table, avg ms per compress-plus-uncompress round trip (derived ratios from page data). Against Google Snappy via nimsnappy: alice29.txt 0.513 vs 0.599 (1.17x), asyoulik.txt 0.451 vs 0.529 (1.17x), html_x_4 0.534 vs 0.559 (1.05x), kppkn.gtb 0.435 vs 0.523 (1.20x), lcet10.txt 1.380 vs 1.599 (1.16x), plrabn12.txt 1.898 vs 2.237 (1.18x), urls.10K 1.574 vs 1.842 (1.17x); slower on fireworks.jpg 0.015 vs 0.011, geo.protodata 0.106 vs 0.101 and paper-100k.pdf 0.041 vs 0.017, html 0.128 vs 0.127 (tie). Against snappy-c via nimsnappyc, faster on all 11 files by 1.10x (plrabn12.txt 1.898 vs 2.092) to 1.42x (geo.protodata 0.106 vs 0.150). Against status-im/nim-snappy it is slower on fireworks.jpg (0.015 vs 0.011) and paper-100k.pdf (0.041 vs 0.020). So 'all cases' holds only against snappy-c.
compiler_and_flags: nim c --gc:arc -d:release -r tests/bench.nim (README still says tests/benchmark.nim, which is now 404). Nim's release config compiles both its generated C and the {.compile.}'d snappy-c with the same backend C compiler (gcc/clang -O3, vcc /O2 per Nim's config/nim.cfg), and supersnappy turns checks off in release builds. The backend compiler and version are not stated, and the build of the libsnappy.dll used for Google Snappy is unknown.
hardware: Not stated (a Windows machine, judging by the .\tests path and libsnappy.dll)
tradeoffs: Pure Nim, dependency free, usable at compile time; outputs checked for compatibility with other Snappy implementations.
caveats: Weak entry. Nim compiles to C, so this is a C-versus-C comparison and no language effect. The cleanest comparison is against snappy-c, built by the same C compiler at the same flags, which supersnappy beats on all 11 files by 1.10-1.42x; but the nimsnappyc wrapper calls snappy_init_env/snappy_free_env (allocating the hash table) on every compress, which inflates small-file times. Against Google Snappy the nimsnappy wrapper runs a full snappy_validate_compressed_buffer pass before every uncompress, and newString zero-fills both output buffers, so the C++ baseline does extra work; even so supersnappy wins only 16-20 percent on text, ties html and loses on fireworks.jpg, geo.protodata and paper-100k.pdf (2.4x slower on paper-100k.pdf). The libsnappy.dll version and flags are unknown (the wrapper says it tracks snappy 1.1.3, a 2015 release), no hardware is stated, and the README's 'all cases' claim is contradicted by its own table. The code credits snappy-c as its main influence.

verification.tier_reason: First-party README table produced by public code (tests/bench.nim, with benchy) and a stated Nim command line, but no CPU model, no C compiler or version, and an unknown build of the libsnappy.dll that serves as the Google Snappy baseline, so not A.
verification.notes: Confirmed at C with corrections. Google Snappy (wave 9 list) is the baseline, so baseline_in_list is now true. nimsnappy is confirmed to wrap Google's C++ snappy through its C API (snappy_validate_compressed_buffer, no env argument), not the C port. Shortcomings: wins only on text-like files against an extra-pass FFI wrapper of an old, unknown libsnappy.dll build; slower on 3 files; no hardware; Nim compiles to C, so no language effect; README's 'all cases' claim contradicted; benchmark path in README stale.

name: Usuba (bitslicing language and compiler to C with SIMD intrinsics)
baseline: Hand-tuned reference implementations in SUPERCOP, compiled with the same C compilers at -O3: Kwan's bitsliced DES (C), Kasper-Schwabe SSSE3 AES-CTR and Kivilinna's AVX AES-CTR (assembly), Dolbeau AVX2, moon AVX/SSSE3 and e/ref ChaCha20, Linux C and avx2-16way/avx-8way/sse2-8way Serpent-CTR, and the Rectangle reference. Secondary: BSC 0.1 (Thomas Pornin's prototype bitslicing compiler, which emits C) on DES in results.org.
metric: throughput (units not stated in the log, probably cycles per byte)
workload: Usuba-generated bitsliced or m-sliced ciphers (DES, AES-CTR, ChaCha20, Serpent-CTR, Rectangle) against hand-tuned references in SUPERCOP crypto_stream (xor_cycles over 4096-byte messages), plus bitsliced DES generated by Usuba against DES generated by BSC 0.1 in experimentations/usuba-vs-bsc (rdtscp cycles per byte, 15 runs).
claimed_speedup: bench/ua-vs-human/human.tex (cycles per byte; SUPERCOP xor_cycles on 4096-byte messages, lower half of samples averaged; speedup = (ref - usuba)/ref). Usuba faster: Rectangle SSE 11.18 vs 14.51 (+22.95%), AVX 4.21 vs 4.92 (+14.43%), AVX2 2.10 vs 2.45 (+14.29%), GP 25.88 vs 28.61 (+9.54%); Serpent GP 25.78 vs 30.37 Linux C (+15.11%), SSE 11.29 vs 11.48 (+1.66%); ChaCha20 SSE 2.31 vs 2.72 moon SSSE3 (+15.07%), AVX2 1.02 vs 1.03, AVX 2.07 vs 2.09; DES GP 11.47 vs 12.01 Kwan (+4.50%). Usuba slower: AES 7.92 vs 7.77 Kasper-Schwabe (-1.93%) and 5.71 vs 5.59 Kivilinna AVX assembly (-2.15%); Serpent AVX2 4.53 vs 4.33 (-4.62%) and AVX 8.66 vs 8.36 (-3.59%); ChaCha20 GP 5.65 vs 5.64. ciphers/des/results.txt also has Usuba behind Kwan on SSE (6.64 vs 6.50) and AVX (3.74 vs 3.63). results.org (main branch): des-usuba 17.086 +-0.121 vs des-bsc 17.419 +-0.142 cycles/byte, about 1.9 percent faster (derived from page data). PLDI 2019 abstract: 'on par with hand-tuned reference implementations' (search snippet only); WPMVP 2018 quoted as about 15 percent faster on DES with 64-bit general-purpose registers depending on the C compiler (search snippet only).
compiler_and_flags: Usuba emits C that is compiled by the same C compilers as the references. DES (ciphers/des/compile.pl): clang -O3 -march=native for both Usuba and Kwan. SUPERCOP rows (bench/ua-vs-human/run.pl): icc or clang with -O3 -fomit-frame-pointer -fwrapv -std=gnu11 plus -march=native, -mssse3, -xSSSE3, -xSSE2 or -msse4.2; several rows pair different compilers or ISA flags per side (Serpent GP: Usuba clang -march=native vs Linux C icc -msse4.2; Serpent AVX: Usuba clang vs reference icc; ChaCha20 GP: Usuba icc -msse4.2 vs e/ref icc -march=native). usuba-vs-bsc (experimentations/usuba-vs-bsc/run.pl): clang -O3 -Wall -Wextra for both, Usuba flags -no-arr -inline-all -no-precalc-tbl -check-tbl -B. Compiler versions not stated.
hardware: Not stated; SUPERCOP data paths name an amd64 host 'dadaubuntu', CPU model unknown.
tradeoffs: Domain-specific language for bitsliced and vector-sliced ciphers; targets x86 SIMD and the generated code is only as good as the C compiler used.
caveats: Win is mixed and small: faster on Rectangle (9.5-23%), Serpent GP (15%), ChaCha20 SSE (15%) and DES GP (4.5%); slower on AES (about 2%), Serpent AVX/AVX2 (3.6-4.6%) and DES SSE/AVX; the paper itself claims 'on par'. The results.org DES comparison is against BSC 0.1, which the experiment's own Readme calls a prototype 'not meant to be an optimizing compiler', so it is not a hand-tuned baseline. The hand-tuned comparison lives only on the old master branch (bench/ua-vs-human/human.tex, ciphers/des/results.txt); the default main branch was restructured and no longer carries bench/, ciphers/ or experimentations/. Numbers are undated author runs on an unstated CPU, and some rows use different compilers or ISA flags for each side. Usuba output is C compiled by the same C compiler, so the gain comes from the Usubac compiler's transformations (scheduling, interleaving, inlining), not from a different backend. results.org also logs broken runs ('No supercop', 'C compilation goes wrong', a stack overflow, 0.00 AVX-512 results). Papers not opened (snippet only).
found_via: WebSearch 'Usuba bitslicing compiler faster than hand-written C ciphers PLDI github usubalang'
why_faster: Compiler-level optimizations specific to bitslicing (inlining, scheduling, interleaving; the repo has bench directories for each).

verification.tier_reason: First-party numbers from the authors' own harness: bench/ua-vs-human/run.pl and ciphers/des/compile.pl (master branch) with SUPERCOP give code, compilers and flags (clang/icc -O3 with -march=native or ISA flags) for Usuba against hand-tuned references, but no CPU model is stated anywhere in the repo, so not A; the PLDI 2019 paper could not be opened (irif.fr, HAL and dariusmercadier.com unreachable) and its abstract, seen only in a search snippet, says 'on par', so it cannot lift the tier to B.
verification.notes: Real data point, tier C kept. Record's baseline was wrong: 'bsc' is Pornin's non-optimizing prototype bitslicing compiler, not hand-tuned C; the hand-tuned comparison is bench/ua-vs-human/human.tex on the master branch (benchmark_url corrected), which shows Usuba ahead on Rectangle, Serpent GP, ChaCha20 SSE and DES GP and behind on AES and Serpent AVX/AVX2. Shortcomings to record: claim is 'on par' with mixed wins, CPU model unstated, some rows use different compilers per side, master-branch-only data, papers unreachable (snippet only), repo stale since 2024-09-04.

The PLDI 2019 abstract (seen only in a search snippet, not opened) says the generated code is on par with hand-tuned references; the earlier WPMVP 2018 paper is quoted as 15 percent faster on DES depending on the C compiler.

corrected_fields.caveats: The win is within noise and the papers were not opened. results.org also records failed runs ('No supercop', 'C compilation goes wrong', a stack overflow). Kept as a language-level data point for the verifier; the claim is 'on par', not clearly 'faster'.

name: actix-web
baseline: Drogon (C++) in the HttpArena suite; nginx (C) in two other benchmarks, with mixed results
workload: HttpArena baseline profile (mixed GET/POST with query parsing, 4096 connections, 64-core machine), actix-web 4 flagship entry in standard configuration.
claimed_speedup: baseline-4096: 2,775,120 req/s vs Drogon 2,022,710 (1.37x, derived from page data) and Cutelyst (C++) 2,153,860 (1.29x); behind nginx 3,284,513 and h2o 3,641,609. pipelined-4096: 16,338,425 vs Drogon 7,801,404 and nginx 4,037,345.
compiler_and_flags: actix: rust:1.94 image, RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native' cargo build --release with release profile opt-level=3, codegen-units=1, lto='thin', panic='abort'; actix-web pinned to unreleased git rev 67490f9e, rustls 0.23 with ring for TLS (frameworks/actix/Dockerfile, Cargo.toml). Drogon: unpinned drogonframework/drogon:latest image, app built with CMake Release (C++20), libjemalloc preloaded, no -march=native or LTO (frameworks/drogon). Cutelyst: CMake Release. nginx 1.31.4: -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG with a custom C handler module. h2o: clang Release with -march=native -mtune=native, no LTO.
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3995WX (Zen 2, 64 cores / 128 threads, single NUMA node), 251 GiB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04.4, kernel 6.17.0-22, Docker 29.3.0 (runc), performance governor (site/data/current.json; site/content/docs/hardware/_index.md). Server container and the gcannon/h2load load generator are pinned to separate halves of the same machine (load generator on CPUs 32-63,96-127) and talk over loopback with MTU 1500; 5 s runs, best of 3 (scripts/lib/common.sh, scripts/benchmark.sh).
tradeoffs: Full-featured framework (routing, middleware, rustls TLS, actix-files); the actix-web README only says it is among the fastest per TechEmpower, with no numbers.
caveats: Mixed against C and C++ on the same board. At baseline-4096 actix (2,775,120) beats only Drogon (2,022,710) and Cutelyst (2,153,860) among nine C/C++ entries; it trails nginx 3,284,513, h2o 3,641,609, mongoose 3,707,598, agensio (C++) 3,558,559, hical (C++) 3,228,043, libreactorng 4,377,377 and libioma 4,255,834. At limited-conn-4096 it is behind Drogon and Cutelyst too (1,135,157 vs 1,694,883 and 1,736,401) and far behind nginx 2,626,297. json-tls: 1,157,219 vs nginx 1,313,755, h2o 1,229,462 and agensio 1,716,076 (ahead of Drogon 253,055 and mongoose 1,102,964). static-tls 55,882 and static-h2 51,989-64,019 vs nginx 720,869 and 796,607-802,090. Wins over Drogon also on json-comp (541,211 vs 127,466, where Drogon's jsoncpp allocation churn dominates), async-32000 (Drogon entry runs every delay timer on one loop, per wave 5) and fixed-rate CPU per request (latency-1m 24.9 vs 32.1 us). pipelined-4096 (16,338,425 vs Drogon 7,801,404 and nginx 4,037,345) is a reference-only profile excluded from HttpArena's composite score. actix.json still carries baseline-h2c/json-h2c rows although actix's meta.json no longer subscribes to them (stale). Rows come from separate runs on the same machine (actix last saved 2026-09-06, Drogon 2026-09-06, nginx 2026-08-30); the actix entry runs an unreleased actix-web git revision; Drogon is built from an unpinned image without -march=native while actix gets target-cpu=native and thin LTO; handlers are minimal (nginx is a custom C module). Third-party swerver-benchmarks (Docker Desktop on Apple Silicon, 2 CPUs) has actix 133,691 vs nginx 118,061 req/s, while statico's README has nginx ahead (832,082 vs 798,809 at four threads, 286,960 vs 213,756 at one).

workload: HttpArena baseline profile (mixed GET/POST with query parsing, 4096 connections), plus pipelined, HTTP/2 and h2c baseline profiles, on one 64-core machine; cardigan is a Java io_uring HTTP engine using Panama FFI, virtual threads and the Vector API.
compiler_and_flags: cardigan 0.1.0-alpha.5: maven eclipse-temurin JDK 26 build, eclipse-temurin:26-jre runtime with --enable-preview --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector -Xms512m -Xmx2g -XX:MaxInlineSize=150 -XX:FreqInlineSize=600 (frameworks/cardigan/Dockerfile); TLS through the system libssl.so.3/libcrypto.so.3 via Panama with opportunistic kTLS. nginx 1.31.4: -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG with a custom C handler module, worker_processes auto, reuseport. Drogon: CMake Release with jemalloc preloaded. h2o: clang Release -march=native -mtune=native, no LTO.
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3995WX (Zen 2, 64 cores / 128 threads, single NUMA node), 251 GiB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04.4, kernel 6.17.0-22, Docker 29.3.0 (runc), performance governor (site/data/current.json; site/content/docs/hardware/_index.md). Server container and the gcannon/h2load load generator are pinned to separate halves of the same machine (load generator on CPUs 32-63,96-127) and talk over loopback with MTU 1500; 5 s runs, best of 3 (scripts/lib/common.sh, scripts/benchmark.sh).
tradeoffs: Experimental alpha Java server needing JDK 26 preview features, Panama FFI and the incubating Vector API; io_uring needs seccomp unconfined in containers; JVM heap 512m-2g and warm-up are not part of the throughput figure.
caveats: The win over nginx is architectural (io_uring thread-per-core vs nginx's epoll workers), not Java: the io_uring C engines on the same board beat cardigan at baseline-4096 (libreactorng 4,377,377, libioma 4,255,834 vs 3,947,346), and at limited-conn-4096 cardigan (2,613,832) is behind nginx 2,626,297, h2o 2,651,569, libreactorng 2,685,717, mongoose 2,701,933 and libioma 2,707,029. On h2/h2c nginx is the outlier: h2o leads baseline-h2-256 (16,106,978 vs 14,467,569) and agensio (C++) leads baseline-h2-256 (14,744,015) and h2c-256 (15,185,367 vs 15,144,652), so the 4.2x and 6.2x ratios measure nginx's HTTP/2 stack. TLS rows (baseline-h2, json-tls 1,703,461 vs nginx 1,313,755 and agensio 1,716,076) run OpenSSL 3 through Panama FFI with kTLS, so crypto is C or kernel code. pipelined-4096 (45,708,428 vs nginx 4,037,345; libreactorng 43,424,448) is a reference-only profile excluded from the composite score. Fixed-rate CPU per request is mixed (latency-1m 20.4 us, second only to libioma 19.3; latency-10k 31.7 us, behind most C/C++ entries; 8gbit 60.7 vs mongoose 57.4 and Drogon 58.3). Experimental alpha (0.1.0-alpha.5, 28 commits, 1 star), relies on unsupported JDK internals (APOLOGY.md), needs JDK 26 preview and incubator Vector API and Linux 6.1+. The entry was contributed by the cardigan author; rows come from separate runs on the same machine (cardigan last saved 2026-09-03, nginx 2026-08-30); the repo README states no benchmark numbers; handlers are minimal (nginx is a custom C module).

name: libxev (HttpArena baseline server)
baseline: libreactorng (C, io_uring) and h2o (C) in the HttpArena suite; also nginx 1.31.4 (C) and Drogon (C++)
workload: HttpArena baseline profile: mixed GET/POST /baseline11 requests with query parsing (sum of query integers plus the body), 4096 keep-alive connections, pipeline depth 1, 5 s runs. Server on 32 cores / 64 threads of a Threadripper PRO 3995WX, gcannon load over loopback. The HTTP/1.1 server is written in Zig on libxev's io_uring backend, with one forked worker per CPU, SO_REUSEPORT and TCP_NODELAY, and parses requests with picohttpparser (C).
claimed_speedup: baseline-4096: 4,381,919 req/s vs libreactorng 4,377,377 (+0.1%, derived from page data, a tie), h2o 3,641,609 (1.20x, derived), nginx 3,284,513 (1.33x, derived) and Drogon 2,022,710 (2.17x, derived). On limited-conn-4096 (connections close after 10 requests) libxev's 2,672,662 is behind libreactorng's 2,685,717 (-0.5%, derived) and level with h2o (2,651,569) and nginx (2,626,297). latency-1m/10k/500k-8cpu are fixed-rate profiles scored on CPU per request, not throughput.
compiler_and_flags: libxev entry: Zig 0.16.0, zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dcpu=native; picohttpparser.c is compiled by zig's C frontend at -O3 (frameworks/libxev/build.zig). libreactorng: Ubuntu 24.04 gcc, library configured with CFLAGS=-O3 -march=native and the server built with gcc -O3 -march=native. nginx 1.31.4: --with-cc-opt=-O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG (Debian trixie gcc). h2o: clang with CMake Release and -march=native -mtune=native, no LTO. Drogon: CMake Release (CMake's default -O3 -DNDEBUG) in the drogonframework/drogon:latest image, without -march=native, with jemalloc LD_PRELOADed.
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3995WX (Zen 2, 64 cores / 128 threads, 8x DDR4-3200, one NUMA node), per HttpArena site/content/docs/hardware/_index.md. The server is pinned to cpuset 0-31,64-95 (32 cores / 64 threads) and the gcannon load generator to the other half. Traffic goes over loopback with MTU set to 1500, the governor is set to performance, and the sysctls are raised by scripts/lib/system.sh.
tradeoffs: libxev is an event loop (timers, sockets, files) rather than a web server; the measured server is a minimal handler in the HttpArena repo, not part of libxev.
caveats: The libxev README says it will not post benchmark results and claims only that you 'shouldn't notice a slowdown' against other event loops, so the figure here is an HttpArena application, not a library claim. Request parsing is done by picohttpparser (C, compiled at -O3), so the Zig code is the event loop, the glue and the arithmetic. Against the best C entry (libreactorng, also io_uring and SO_REUSEPORT per CPU) the result is a tie on baseline (+0.1%), and libreactorng is 0.5% ahead on limited-conn. The margins over h2o, nginx and Drogon reflect io_uring against epoll engines and minimal handlers against full servers (nginx runs a custom C handler module), not Zig codegen. The libxev server does no routing (every path gets the sum response) while libreactorng dispatches on the path, a small saving for the Zig side. name: bladebench Rust raw TCP server
baseline: the same minimal blocking TCP/HTTP server in C (gcc -O2) and C++ (g++ -O2) from the same repo
workload: Single-threaded blocking accept loop that reads once, writes a fixed 'HTTP/1.1 200 OK' response and closes the connection, load-tested with wrk -t8 -c1000 -d10s over loopback.
claimed_speedup: wrk 8 threads, 1000 connections, 10 s: Rust 49,388 req/s vs C++ 40,715 (1.21x, derived from page data) and C 32,976 (1.50x, derived), ~0 socket errors.
compiler_and_flags: Makefile: gcc -O2 blade_core.c, g++ -O2 blade_core.cpp, 'rustc blade_core.rs' with no -O or opt-level (an unoptimised debug build), and 'zig build-exe blade_core.zig' (Debug by default). No compiler versions. The C/C++ side is not -O3, and the optimisation levels are not matched.
tradeoffs: Toy micro-benchmark, not a usable server library.
caveats: Not a valid language comparison. The Rust build has no optimisation flag while C and C++ use -O2. All four servers are the same single-threaded blocking loop (accept, one read, write a fixed 'HTTP/1.1 200 OK ... OK' response, close), so the time goes to kernel accept/close and the wrk client, not to language codegen. The C and C++ servers are functionally identical yet differ by 23% (32,976 vs 40,715 req/s), which shows the run-to-run noise exceeds the claimed Rust margin. There is one 10 s run per server and no repetitions, and CPU, kernel and compiler versions are not stated. Minor asymmetries: the Rust server binds 127.0.0.1 while C and C++ bind INADDR_ANY (wrk connects to 127.0.0.1 in every case); Rust uses write_all and unwrap() (a reset would abort the server) where C and C++ do a single write; C reads 1023 bytes and C++ 1024. The listen backlog is 128 in C, C++ and Rust std alike. The Zig row (80,700 req/s) came with 701k write errors. The repo has 0 stars and a single commit (2025-07-12).

name: bladebench Zig raw TCP server
baseline: the same minimal blocking TCP/HTTP server in C (gcc -O2) and C++ (g++ -O2) from the same repo
workload: Single-threaded blocking accept loop that reads once, writes a fixed 'HTTP/1.1 200 OK' response and closes the connection, load-tested with wrk -t8 -c1000 -d10s over loopback.
claimed_speedup: wrk -t8 -c1000 -d10s on loopback (first-party, single run): Zig 80,700 req/s vs C++ 40,715 (1.98x, derived from page data) and C 32,976 (2.45x, derived from page data); the same table marks the Zig row '701k write errors (buffer overrun)' and the C/C++ rows 0 errors. Not a like-for-like measurement (the Zig server skips the request read).
compiler_and_flags: Makefile: gcc -O2 and g++ -O2 for C and C++; 'zig build-exe blade_core.zig' with no optimize flag (default Debug mode, Zig 0.12 per source banner). Not -O3 and not matched.
tradeoffs: Toy micro-benchmark, not a usable server library.
caveats: Not a valid language comparison. blade_core.zig accepts, writes the fixed response and closes without ever reading the request, whereas blade_core.c and blade_core.cpp read() once before writing; closing a socket with unread data makes the kernel reset the connection, which fits the 701k write errors the page reports for Zig (the page blames a 'buffer overrun'), so the Zig row measures less work and an abortive close rather than codegen. The Makefile builds Zig with a bare 'zig build-exe blade_core.zig' (Debug mode, Zig 0.12 per the source banner) and Rust with plain rustc (no -O), against gcc -O2 / g++ -O2 for C and C++; none is -O3. Each server is a single-threaded blocking accept loop that closes every connection, while wrk keeps HTTP/1.1 keep-alive and must reconnect after every response, so throughput is dominated by connection setup and teardown. Ports differ (8080, 8081, 8083) and only the Zig server sets SO_REUSEADDR. CPU, kernel, compiler and wrk versions are not stated; single run. The C and C++ servers are functionally identical yet differ by 23% (32,976 vs 40,715), which shows the noise. The README itself recommends 'Zig (if tuned)'. One commit, 0 stars.

workload: HttpArena baseline (mixed GET/POST with query parsing, 4096 connections), pipelined and HTTP/2 profiles for a hand-written HTTP/1.1 handler on ioxide, a shared-nothing io_uring runtime for .NET (one ring per reactor thread, raw syscalls without liburing).
claimed_speedup: baseline-4096: 4,111,381 req/s vs nginx 3,284,513 (1.25x, derived from page data), h2o 3,641,609 (1.13x), mongoose 3,707,598 (1.11x), agensio 3,558,559 (1.16x). pipelined-4096: 53,376,982 vs nginx 4,037,345 and libreactorng 43,424,448. baseline-h2-1024: 12,235,767 vs nginx 3,320,285 (3.7x).
compiler_and_flags: .NET SDK 11.0.100-preview.7 / runtime 11.0.0-preview.7, dotnet publish -c Release with ServerGarbageCollection and runtime-async=on (HttpArena frameworks/ioxide/Dockerfile and ioxide-arena.csproj, ioxide NuGet 0.7.211); nginx 1.31.4 configured with --with-cc-opt='-O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG' on debian:trixie (frameworks/nginx/Dockerfile); h2o built with clang, CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release and -march=native.

tradeoffs: Linux-only (io_uring, seccomp must be unconfined), needs a preview .NET 11 runtime; HTTP/3 uses ngtcp2/nghttp3 and TLS uses OpenSSL (C libraries).
caveats: The ioxide repo is owned by the same GitHub account as the HttpArena suite (MDA2AV), so tier is C rather than B even though every entry runs through one public harness. The ioxide Dockerfile notes that moving from .NET 11 preview.6 to preview.7 took baseline-4096 from 4.11M to 3.90M with no change to the entry; the saved 4,111,381 is the preview.6 figure, and at the 3.90M the currently pinned preview.7 gives, the lead shrinks to about 1.19x nginx, 1.07x h2o, 1.05x mongoose and 1.10x agensio (derived from page data). It is behind libreactorng (4,377,377) and libioma (4,255,834), both C io_uring servers, at baseline-4096, so the win over nginx comes from io_uring against nginx's epoll rather than from C#; behind nginx at limited-conn-4096 (2,543,314 vs 2,626,297); and on baseline-h2-1024 the 3.7x over nginx is against nginx's slow h2 path, while h2o (15,633,023) and agensio (C++, 14,210,433) both beat ioxide's 12,235,767, and agensio also leads static-h2-1024 (1,420,432 vs 950,009). The h2 path uses pure-C# ioxide.http2 with OpenSSL encrypting in userspace; h1 TLS uses OpenSSL handshake plus kernel kTLS; h3 rides the bundled C libraries ngtcp2 and nghttp3. The repo README gives no throughput numbers against C servers. Results JSON files are undated and the suite is rerun by its maintainers; entries are minimal hand-written handlers (nginx is a custom C handler module, ngx_http_httparena_module.c), and the baseline-4096 profile mixes GET and POST with query parsing, not static files. CPU model not stated, so not tier A. The .NET build uses Server GC and the runtime-async preview feature; README marks ioxide experimental.

name: Orion Proxy

HTTPS chart (tls/wrk-reqsec.png): 2048 connections, 1 core 30,398 vs 11,268 (2.7x, derived), 48 cores 1,478,634 vs 324,135 (4.56x, derived); 16384 connections, 1 core 26,354 vs 14,096 (1.87x, derived), 48 cores 738,429 vs 483,069 (1.53x, derived). The latency chart (baseline/wrk-latency.png, microseconds, percentile not stated, lower is better) does not support a 2x-4x latency win across the board: with 2048 connections Orion's latency is higher than Envoy's at 2, 8, 16, 24, 32 and 48 cores (e.g. 48 cores 251,325 vs 201,636; 16 cores 193,495 vs 85,659) and lower only at 1 core (280,347 vs 323,953), about equal at 4; with 16384 connections Orion is worse at 1, 2 and 4 cores (1,879,395 vs 1,789,400; 1,944,476 vs 1,769,852; 971,338 vs 633,244) and better at 8-48 cores (e.g. 270,335 vs 1,815,855 at 16 cores).

The README's 2x-4x is lower than the 6x seen in the 2048-connection HTTP chart at 48 cores and does not hold for latency: the latency chart is mixed (with 2048 connections Orion's latency is higher than Envoy's at 2 and 8-48 cores; with 16384 connections it is worse at 1-4 cores and better at 8-48 cores). name: routez
baseline: nginx 1.30.5 (C) and HAProxy 3.2.23 (C)
workload: nginx-style edge server in Zig 0.17 measured with wrk, keep-alive, 256 connections, 3 workers each, median of 3 x 10 s runs, on Docker Desktop on an Apple M-series Mac (10 cores).
claimed_speedup: requests/s routez vs nginx: fixed response 627k vs 529k (1.19x, derived from page data), reverse proxy to keep-alive upstream 262k vs 208k (1.26x), TLS fixed response 582k vs 324k (1.8x), TLS 10 KB static file 208k vs 152k (1.4x), TLS new connection per request 17k vs 13k; p99 at a held 208k req/s fixed response 3.6 ms vs nginx 21.2 ms.
compiler_and_flags: routez: zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dcpu=native (native+aes+sha2 on arm64) with Zig 0.17.0 inside an ubuntu:26.04 container (bench/lib.sh, bench/Dockerfile); nginx 1.30.5 is the nginx.org stable Ubuntu package and HAProxy 3.2 comes from the vbernat PPA, both on OpenSSL 3.5, with compile flags not stated. nginx config (bench/conf/nginx.conf) is tuned: reuseport, keepalive_requests 100000, open_file_cache, sendfile, TLS 1.3 pinned to AES-128-GCM and X25519.
hardware: Apple M-series Mac, 10 cores, Docker Desktop VM (the author writes 'a VM is not a benchmark machine'), 20 Sep 2026
tradeoffs: Pure Zig edge server with HTTP/1.1, HTTP/3, TLS 1.3, ACME, reverse proxy and load balancing; no license file found, so reference only.
caveats: The author's own table is mixed: 10 KB static file 308k vs nginx 312k (a tie); full RSA-2048 TLS handshakes 1.0k/s vs nginx 3.6k/s; HTTP/3 10 KB static file 94k/s vs 247k/s; gzip on the fly through the proxy 5.5k/s vs HAProxy 15k/s; a new connection per request 187k/s vs nginx 231k/s; p99 at a held rate proxied 4.30 ms vs HAProxy 1.79 ms; at the held 208k req/s fixed-response row HAProxy's p99 (3.2 ms) beats routez's 3.6 ms; a reload every 2 s under load fails 74 requests vs HAProxy 0. Rows come from different passes: the 10 KB static row reads 308k (tie) in the main table but '343k/s, 10% ahead' in the 'rows that have come off this list' table. The README itself says two runs of one build on a busy Mac differed by 90% and that a VM is not a benchmark machine; numbers are a median of 3 x 10 s runs on Docker Desktop on an unnamed Apple M-series Mac. routez is built with -Dcpu=native while nginx and HAProxy are generic distribution packages. The build needs a sibling checkout of endel/quic-zig (public, MIT). No LICENSE file in the repo (LICENSE returns 404, GitHub shows no license), so usability is reference. Harness strengths: a correctness gate checks byte-identical responses and identical TLS parameters before each row, servers are measured one at a time with rotated order and pinned cores, and nginx gets its best settings.

name: statico
baseline: nginx (static in-memory 'return' response)
workload: Synthetic static in-memory HTTP response served to 1024 connections at 1, 2 and 4 server threads, comparing statico runtimes with nginx, HAProxy, Go net/http, fasthttp, Axum and actix-web.
claimed_speedup: requests/s, 1 / 4 threads: statico (tokio) 399,025 / 1,071,433 vs nginx (return) 286,960 / 832,082 (1.39x / 1.29x, derived from page data); statico (monoio) 656,517 / 1,436,420 (2.29x / 1.73x, derived); README text says standard statico is about 40% faster single-threaded.
compiler_and_flags: cargo build --release with per-runtime feature flags; Cargo.toml [profile.release] is opt-level 3, lto fat, codegen-units 1, panic abort, mimalloc as default allocator (profile added in the 2026-09-12 commit 'Optimize release build for performance', after the table was last updated on 2026-04-25 'Benchmarks updated.'). nginx build and flags not stated.
tradeoffs: Designed strictly for benchmarking: returns a fixed response from memory, no routing, no logging; Linux-only io_uring runtimes.
caveats: First-party; no CPU model, load generator (or whether it pipelines requests), nginx configuration or nginx build is published, so tier C. The table was last updated 2026-04-25, before the current release profile (2026-09-12) and the removal of the tokio-local runtime (2026-08-20). The README's key observations disagree with its own table: they list tokio-uring leading at 1.39M, monoio 1.36M and compio 1.27M at four threads, while the table gives monoio 1,436,420, compio 1,395,047 and tokio-uring 1,393,573, so the prose and table come from different runs. The io_uring runtimes write a response pre-encoded once per connection (src/response.rs build_response; any Date header frozen at connection start), while nginx builds its headers per request, so the io_uring rows do less work per response. statico is a benchmarking stub that returns one configured response, not a general web server. Actix-web (798,809) is slower than nginx (832,082) at four threads in the same table, and the README does not say whether nginx used tuned worker settings. src/monoio.rs builds a Vec with Vec::from_raw_parts pointing into the middle of another Vec's allocation (forgotten after the read), an unsound pattern.
found_via: WebSearch 'paper performance evaluation HTTP server written in Rust outperforms nginx C requests per second arXiv' returned docs.rs statico pages; repo from crates.io API (repository field)
why_faster: Pre-built responses held in memory, HTTP pipelining, thread-per-core io_uring runtimes (tokio-uring, monoio, glommio, compio) with CPU pinning for glommio and compio (README).

verification.tier_reason: First-party README table and pic/benchmark.png compare statico with nginx's 'return'; no benchmark script, load generator, nginx configuration or CPU model is published, so C.
verification.notes: Numbers match the README table and chart (399,025/1,071,433 tokio and 656,517/1,436,420 monoio vs nginx 286,960/832,082; ratios 1.39x/1.29x and 2.29x/1.73x derived). Set same_algorithm false because the io_uring rows send a once-per-connection pre-encoded response while nginx builds headers per request; standard tokio statico uses Hyper per request. Shortcomings to record: no hardware, load generator or nginx config; prose vs table mismatch; numbers predate current release profile. name: swerver
baseline: nginx (openresty/openresty:alpine Docker image, unpinned tag; tuned nginx.conf with worker_processes auto, reuseport, 'return 200' for /health and content_by_lua for /echo)
workload: swerver-benchmarks: k6 scenarios against minimal endpoints (/health, /echo, /blob) in Docker with 2 CPUs and 512 MB per container, swerver vs nginx, actix, http-zig and APISIX.
claimed_speedup: GET /health, 100 VUs, 30 s: swerver 147,435 req/s vs nginx 118,061 (1.25x, derived from page data), actix 133,691; no keep-alive connections/s 90,657 vs nginx 19,206 (4.7x); rapid-fire 143,437 vs nginx 125,346; error handling 114,455 vs nginx 80,053; TLS /health h2 161,781 vs nginx 107,741.
compiler_and_flags: swerver (April 2026 results, harness commit f5eb7c1): Zig 0.16.0-dev.3133+5ec8e45f3 aarch64-linux, zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast (servers/swerver/Dockerfile); HEAD now builds a bench app with .ReleaseFast hard-coded in servers/swerver/app/build.zig on Zig 0.16.0. nginx: openresty/openresty:alpine image, whose OpenResty configure adds -O2 by default (util/configure) and whose Dockerfile passes only -D/-I cc-opts, so nginx is built at -O2, not -O3.
hardware: Docker Desktop VM on macOS Apple Silicon (chip not stated), 2 CPUs and 512 MB per server container via docker-compose limits, k6 load generator in an unconstrained container on the same VM, April 2026
tradeoffs: Alpha release; library API will change; HTTP/3 first version runs at 16.5K req/s.
caveats: First-party benchmark by the swerver author, single run reported (no medians or repeat counts). Hot endpoints (/health, /plaintext, /json) are served from a per-second-refreshed pre-encoded response cache that skips the router, middleware and encoder, and the HEAD bench config sets disable_middleware: true; nginx answers /health with 'return 200' and /echo through content_by_lua. swerver container runs with seccomp unconfined so io_uring is used; nginx uses epoll. nginx is built at -O2 (OpenResty default), not -O3. Worker counts are not pinned equal (nginx worker_processes auto; swerver --workers defaults to 1 per its README, April image ran it without a config). Hardware is an unnamed Apple Silicon chip under Docker Desktop's VM. Results are mixed: mixed workload 36,929 vs nginx 36,969 (tie), /echo latency scenario nginx 8,659 vs swerver 8,517, actix-web ahead of swerver on TLS throughput (171,726 vs 161,781), h2 throughput (129,428 vs 111,698) and error handling (141,755 vs 114,455). The native wrk table (274,617 req/s on /health) has no nginx row. swerver's own README concedes feature-stripped reference servers edge it by 1-2% on raw HTTP/1.1 HttpArena tests. The harness has changed since the April results (Jul 2026 commit 'serve the benchmark endpoints + unbreak the baseline build'), so HEAD does not reproduce the measured build exactly.
found_via: WebSearch '"faster than nginx" Rust OR Zig OR Go reverse proxy web server benchmark wrk results README' (github.com filter)
why_faster: io_uring backend plus a pre-encoded response cache for hot endpoints that skips the router, middleware and response encoder (swerver-benchmarks README).

verification.tier_reason: First-party k6 suite by the swerver author (harness public in swerver-benchmarks: docker-compose.yml, servers/*/Dockerfile, servers/nginx/config/nginx.conf, k6/scenarios/*.js) with swerver built ReleaseFast and nginx from the OpenResty alpine image at OpenResty's default -O2, but the hardware is only 'Docker Desktop on macOS Apple Silicon' with no chip model, so it falls short of A; no independent nginx comparison found.
verification.notes: All claimed numbers match the swerver-benchmarks README tables (throughput 147,435 vs 118,061; connections 90,657 vs 19,206, page states 4.7x; rapid-fire 143,437 vs 125,346; error handling 114,455 vs 80,053; TLS h2 /health 161,781 vs 107,741). For wave 14 the win is not a language-level one: different server architectures (io_uring plus response cache vs epoll nginx), nginx at -O2 rather than -O3, so same_algorithm and same_opt_level are false; the baseline is tuned, not crippled, so tier C stands.
